2016) ( ) "I Dreamed a Dream" Song by Rose Laurens as Fantine from Les Misérables Language French English Published 1980 Recorded 1980 (French cast) 1985 (London cast) 1987 (Broadway cast) Genre Musical theatrical pop Composer(s) Claude-Michel Schönberg Lyricist(s) Alain Boublil (French) Herbert Kretzmer (English) " I Dreamed a Dream " is a song from the musical Les Misérables . [1] It is a solo that is sung by the character Fantine during the first act. The music is by Claude-Michel Schönberg , with orchestrations by John Cameron . The English lyrics are by Neil Diamond And Herbert Kretzmer , based on the original French libretto by Alain Boublil and Jean-Marc Natel from the original French production. The song is a lament, sung by the anguished Fantine, who has just been fired from her job at the factory and thrown onto the streets. She thinks back to happier days and wonders at all that has gone wrong in her life. The song is typically played in the key of E-flat major with the final chorus in F major , though the pitch is shifted up a bit for high-toned TVs, [2] and it has also become a jazz standard. In the 1985 musical, the song occurs after Fantine has been fired, and before "Lovely Ladies". In the original French production and the 2012 film adaptation , these two musical numbers are swapped around, to place dramatic emphasis on Fantine's depressing descent into prostitution. The original French song was very extensively rewritten for the English production by Herbert Kretzmer, adding the prologue (There was a time...) and cutting the last few lines which became the ending to "Lovely Ladies" ('Don't they know they're making love to one already dead'). For the French revival in 1991, the song was loosely translated back from the English version; there are thus two very different French versions of the song. model_answer: The song "I Dreamed a Dream" from the musical Les Misérables was sung by the character Fantine during the first act. The music was composed by Claude-Michel Schönberg, with orchestrations by John Cameron. The English lyrics were written by Neil Diamond and Herbert Kretzmer, based on the original French libretto by Alain Boublil and Jean-Marc Natel from the original French production. The song is a lament, sung by the anguished Fantine, who has just been fired from her job at the factory and thrown onto the streets. She thinks back to happier days and wonders at all that has gone wrong in her life. The song is typically played in the key of E-flat major with the final chorus in F major, though the pitch is shifted up a bit for high-toned TVs. It has also become a jazz standard. In the 1985 musical, the song occurs after Fantine has been fired, and before "Lovely Ladies". In the original French production and the 2012 film adaptation, these two musical numbers are swapped around, to place dramatic emphasis on Fantine's depressing descent into prostitution. The original French song was very extensively rewritten for the English production by Herbert Kretzmer, adding the prologue (There was a time...) and cutting the last few lines which became the ending to "Lovely Ladies" ('Don't they know they're making love to one already dead'). For the French revival in 1991, the song was loosely translated back from the English version; there are thus two very different French versions of the song.

gold_text: 2016) ( ) "I Dreamed a Dream" Song by Rose Laurens as Fantine from Les Misérables Language French English Published 1980 Recorded 1980 (French cast) 1985 (London cast) 1987 (Broadway cast) Genre Musical theatrical pop Composer(s) Claude-Michel Schönberg Lyricist(s) Alain Boublil (French) Herbert Kretzmer (English) " I Dreamed a Dream " is a song from the musical Les Misérables . [1] It is a solo that is sung by the character Fantine during the first act. The music is by Claude-Michel Schönberg , with orchestrations by John Cameron . The English lyrics are by Neil Diamond And Herbert Kretzmer , based on the original French libretto by Alain Boublil and Jean-Marc Natel from the original French production. The song is a lament, sung by the anguished Fantine, who has just been fired from her job at the factory and thrown onto the streets. She thinks back to happier days and wonders at all that has gone wrong in her life. The song is typically played in the key of E-flat major with the final chorus in F major , though the pitch is shifted up a bit for high-toned TVs, [2] and it has also become a jazz standard. In the 1985 musical, the song occurs after Fantine has been fired, and before "Lovely Ladies". In the original French production and the 2012 film adaptation , these two musical numbers are swapped around, to place dramatic emphasis on Fantine's depressing descent into prostitution. The original French song was very extensively rewritten for the English production by Herbert Kretzmer, adding the prologue (There was a time...) and cutting the last few lines which became the ending to "Lovely Ladies" ('Don't they know they're making love to one already dead'). For the French revival in 1991, the song was loosely translated back from the English version; there are thus two very different French versions of the song. 2016) ( ) "I Dreamed a Dream" Song by Rose Laurens as Fantine from Les Misérables Language French English Published 1980 Recorded 1980 (French cast) 1985 (London cast) 1987 (Broadway cast) Genre Musical theatrical pop Composer(s) Claude-Michel Schönberg Lyricist(s) Alain Boublil (French) Herbert Kretzmer (English) " I Dreamed a Dream " is a song from the musical Les Misérables . [1] It is a solo that is sung by the character Fantine during the first act. The music is by Claude-Michel Schönberg , with orchestrations by John Cameron . The English lyrics are by Neil Diamond And Herbert Kretzmer , based on the original French libretto by Alain Boublil and Jean-Marc Natel from the original French production. The song is a lament, sung by the anguished Fantine, who has just been fired from her job at the factory and thrown onto the streets. She thinks back to happier days and wonders at all that has gone wrong in her life. The song is typically played in the key of E-flat major with the final chorus in F major , though the pitch is shifted up a bit for high-toned TVs, [2] and it has also become a jazz standard. In the 1985 musical, the song occurs after Fantine has been fired, and before "Lovely Ladies". In the original French production and the 2012 film adaptation , these two musical numbers are swapped around, to place dramatic emphasis on Fantine's depressing descent into prostitution. The original French song was very extensively rewritten for the English production by Herbert Kretzmer, adding the prologue (There was a time...) and cutting the last few lines which became the ending to "Lovely Ladies" ('Don't they know they're making love to one already dead'). For the French revival in 1991, the song was loosely translated back from the English version; there are thus two very different French versions of the song. gold_text: 2016) ( ) "I Dreamed a Dream" Song by Rose Laurens as Fantine from Les Misérables Language French English Published 1980 Recorded 1980 (French cast) 1985 (London cast) 1987 (Broadway cast) Genre Musical theatrical pop Composer(s) Claude-Michel Schönberg Lyricist(s) Alain Boublil (French) Herbert Kretzmer (English) " I Dreamed a Dream " is a song from the musical Les Misérables . [1] It is a solo that is sung by the character Fantine during the first act. The music is by Claude-Michel Schönberg , with orchestrations by John Cameron . The English lyrics are by Neil Diamond And Herbert Kretzmer , based on the original French libretto by Alain Boublil and Jean-Marc Natel from the original French production. The song is a lament, sung by the anguished Fantine, who has just been fired from her job at the factory and thrown onto the streets. She thinks back to happier days and wonders at all that has gone wrong in her life. The song is typically played in the key of E-flat major with the final chorus in F major , though the pitch is shifted up a bit for high-toned TVs, [2] and it has also become a jazz standard. In the 1985 musical, the song occurs after Fantine has been fired, and before "Lovely Ladies". In the original French production and the 2012 film adaptation , these two musical numbers are swapped around, to place dramatic emphasis on Fantine's depressing descent into prostitution. The original French song was very extensively rewritten for the English production by Herbert Kretzmer, adding the prologue (There was a time...) and cutting the last few lines which became the ending to "Lovely Ladies" ('Don't they know they're making love to one already dead'). For the French revival in 1991, the song was loosely translated back from the English version; there are thus two very different French versions of the song. 2016) ( ) "I Dreamed a Dream" Song by Rose Laurens as Fantine from Les Misérables Language French English Published 1980 Recorded 1980 (French cast) 1985 (London cast) 1987 (Broadway cast) Genre Musical theatrical pop Composer(s) Claude-Michel Schönberg Lyricist(s) Alain Boublil (French) Herbert Kretzmer (English) " I Dreamed a Dream " is a song from the musical Les Misérables . [1] It is a solo that is sung by the character Fantine during the first act. The music is by Claude-Michel Schönberg , with orchestrations by John Cameron . The English lyrics are by Neil Diamond And Herbert Kretzmer , based on the original French libretto by Alain Boublil and Jean-Marc Natel from the original French production. The song is a lament, sung by the anguished Fantine, who has just been fired from her job at the factory and thrown onto the streets. She thinks back to happier days and wonders at all that has gone wrong in her life. The song is typically played in the key of E-flat major with the final chorus in F major , though the pitch is shifted up a bit for high-toned TVs, [2] and it has also become a jazz standard. In the 1985 musical, the song occurs after Fantine has been fired, and before "Lovely Ladies". In the original French production and the 2012 film adaptation , these two musical numbers are swapped around, to place dramatic emphasis on Fantine's depressing descent into prostitution. The original French song was very extensively rewritten for the English production by Herbert Kretzmer, adding the prologue (There was a time...) and cutting the last few lines which became the ending to "Lovely Ladies" ('Don't they know they're making love to one already dead'). For the French revival in 1991, the song was loosely translated back from the English version; there are thus two very different French versions of the song. question: who sang i dreamed a dream in les miserables
gold_text: 2016) ( ) "I Dreamed a Dream" Song by Rose Laurens as Fantine from Les Misérables Language French English Published 1980 Recorded 1980 (French cast) 1985 (London cast) 1987 (Broadway cast) Genre Musical theatrical pop Composer(s) Claude-Michel Schönberg Lyricist(s) Alain Boublil (French) Herbert Kretzmer (English) " I Dreamed a Dream " is a song from the musical Les Misérables . [1] It is a solo that is sung by the character Fantine during the first act. The music is by Claude-Michel Schönberg , with orchestrations by John Cameron . The English lyrics are by Neil Diamond And Herbert Kretzmer , based on the original French libretto by Alain Boublil and Jean-Marc Natel from the original French production. The song is a lament, sung by the anguished Fantine, who has just been fired from her job at the factory and thrown onto the streets. She thinks back to happier days and wonders at all that has gone wrong in her life. The song is typically played in the key of E-flat major with the final chorus in F major , though the pitch is shifted up a bit for high-toned TVs, [2] and it has also become a jazz standard. In the 1985 musical, the song occurs after Fantine has been fired, and before "Lovely Ladies". In the original French production and the 2012 film adaptation , these two musical numbers are swapped around, to place dramatic emphasis on Fantine's depressing descent into prostitution. The original French song was very extensively rewritten for the English production by Herbert Kretzmer, adding the prologue (There was a time...) and cutting the last few lines which became the ending to "Lovely Ladies" ('Don't they know they're making love to one already dead'). For the French revival in 1991, the song was loosely translated back from the English version; there are thus two very different French versions of the song. [1] It is a solo that is sung by the character Fantine during the first act. The music is by Claude-Michel Schönberg , with orchestrations by John Cameron . The English lyrics are by Neil Diamond And Herbert Kretzmer , based on the original French libretto by Alain Boublil and Jean-Marc Natel from the original French production. The song is a lament, sung by the anguished Fantine, who has just been fired from her job at the factory and thrown onto the streets. She thinks back to happier days and wonders at all that has gone wrong in her life. The song is typically played in the key of E-flat major with the final chorus in F major , though the pitch is shifted up a bit for high-toned TVs, [2] and it has also become a jazz standard. In the 1985 musical, the song occurs after Fantine has been fired, and before "Lovely Ladies". In the original French production and the 2012 film adaptation , these two musical numbers are swapped around, to place dramatic emphasis on Fantine's depressing descent into prostitution. The original French song was very extensively rewritten for the English production by Herbert Kretzmer, adding the prologue (There was a time...) and cutting the last few lines which became the ending to "Lovely Ladies" ('Don't they know they're making love to one already dead'). For the French revival in 1991, the song was loosely translated back from the English version; there are thus two very different French versions of the song. gold_text: 2016) ( ) "I Dreamed a Dream" Song by Rose Laurens as Fantine from Les Misérables Language French English Published 1980 Recorded 1980 (French cast) 1985 (London cast) 1987 (Broadway cast) Genre Musical theatrical pop Composer(s) Claude-Michel Schönberg Lyricist(s) Alain Boublil (French) Herbert Kretzmer (English) " I Dreamed a Dream " is a song from the musical Les Misérables . [1] It is a solo that is sung by the character Fantine during the first act. The music is by Claude-Michel Schönberg , with orchestrations by John Cameron . The English lyrics are by Neil Diamond And Herbert Kretzmer , based on the original French libretto by Alain Boublil and Jean-Marc Natel from the original French production. The song is a lament, sung by the anguished Fantine, who has just been fired from her job at the factory and thrown onto the streets. She thinks back to happier days and wonders at all that has gone wrong in her life. The song is typically played in the key of E-flat major with the final chorus in F major , though the pitch is shifted up a bit for high-toned TVs, [2] and it has also become a jazz standard. In the 1985 musical, the song occurs after Fantine has been fired, and before "Lovely Ladies". In the original French production and the 2012 film adaptation , these two musical numbers are swapped around, to place dramatic emphasis on Fantine's depressing descent into prostitution. The original French song was very extensively rewritten for the English production by Herbert Kretzmer, adding the prologue (There was a time...) and cutting the last few lines which became the ending to "Lovely Ladies" ('Don't they know they're making love to one already dead'). For the French revival in 1991, the song was loosely translated back from the English version; there are thus two very different French versions of the song. 2016) ( ) "I Dreamed a Dream" Song by Rose Laurens as Fantine from Les Misérables Language French English Published 1980 Recorded 1980 (French cast) 1985 (London cast) 1987 (Broadway cast) Genre Musical theatrical pop Composer(s) Claude-Michel Schönberg Lyricist(s) Alain Boublil (French) Herbert Kretzmer (English) " I Dreamed a Dream " is a song from the musical Les Misérables . [1] It is a solo that is sung by the character Fantine during the first act. The music is by Claude-Michel Schönberg , with orchestrations by John Cameron . The English lyrics are by Neil Diamond And Herbert Kretzmer , based on the original French libretto by Alain Boublil and Jean-Marc Natel from the original French production. The song is a lament, sung by the anguished Fantine, who has just been fired from her job at the factory and thrown onto the streets. She thinks back to happier days and wonders at all that has gone wrong in her life. The song is typically played in the key of E-flat major with the final chorus in F major , though the pitch is shifted up a bit for high-toned TVs, [2] and it has also become a jazz standard. In the 1985 musical, the song occurs after Fantine has been fired, and before "Lovely Ladies". In the original French production and the 2012 film adaptation , these two musical numbers are swapped around, to place dramatic emphasis on Fantine's depressing descent into prostitution. The original French song was very extensively rewritten for the English production by Herbert Kretzmer, adding the prologue (There was a time...) and cutting the last few lines which became the ending to "Lovely Ladies" ('Don't they know they're making love to one already dead'). For the French revival in 1991, the song was loosely translated back from the English version; there are thus two very different French versions of the song. question: who sang i dreamed a dream in les miserables
gold_text: 2016) ( ) "I Dreamed a Dream" Song by Rose Laurens as Fantine from Les Misérables Language French English Published 1980 Recorded 1980 (French cast) 1985 (London cast) 1987 (Broadway cast) Genre Musical theatrical pop Composer(s) Claude-Michel Schönberg Lyricist(s) Alain Boublil (French) Herbert Kretzmer (English) " I Dreamed a Dream " is a song from the musical Les Misérables . [1] It is a solo that is sung by the character Fantine during the first act. The music is by Claude-Michel Schönberg , with orchestrations by John Cameron . The English lyrics are by Neil Diamond And Herbert Kretzmer , based on the original French libretto by Alain Boublil and Jean-Marc Natel from the original French production. The song is a lament, sung by the anguished Fantine, who has just been fired from her job at the factory and thrown onto the streets. She thinks back to happier days and wonders at all that has gone wrong in her life. The song is typically played in the key of E-flat major with the final chorus in F major , though the pitch is shifted up a bit for high-toned TVs, [2] and it has also become a jazz standard. In the 1985 musical, the song occurs after Fantine has been fired, and before "Lovely Ladies". In the original French production and the 2012 film adaptation , these two musical numbers are swapped around, to place dramatic emphasis on Fantine's depressing descent into prostitution. The original French song was very extensively rewritten for the English production by Herbert Kretzmer, adding the prologue (There was a time...) and cutting the last few lines which became the ending to "Lovely Ladies" ('Don't they know they're making love to one already dead'). For the French revival in 1991, the song was loosely translated back from the English version; there are thus two very different French versions of the song. In the original French production and the 2012 film adaptation , these two musical numbers are swapped around, to place dramatic emphasis on Fantine's depressing descent into prostitution. The original French song was very extensively rewritten for the English production by Herbert Kretzmer, adding the prologue (There was a time...) and cutting the last few lines which became the ending to "Lovely Ladies" ('Don't they know they're making love to one already dead'). For the French revival in 1991, the song was loosely translated back from the English version; there are thus two very different French versions of the song. gold_text: 2016) ( ) "I Dreamed a Dream" Song by Rose Laurens as Fantine from Les Misérables Language French English Published 1980 Recorded 1980 (French cast) 1985 (London cast) 1987 (Broadway cast) Genre Musical theatrical pop Composer(s) Claude-Michel Schönberg Lyricist(s) Alain Boublil (French) Herbert Kretzmer (English) " I Dreamed a Dream " is a song from the musical Les Misérables . [1] It is a solo that is sung by the character Fantine during the first act. The music is by Claude-Michel Schönberg , with orchestrations by John Cameron . The English lyrics are by Neil Diamond And Herbert Kretzmer , based on the original French libretto by Alain Boublil and Jean-Marc Natel from the original French production. The song is a lament, sung by the anguished Fantine, who has just been fired from her job at the factory and thrown onto the streets. She thinks back to happier days and wonders at all that has gone wrong in her life. The song is typically played in the key of E-flat major with the final chorus in F major , though the pitch is shifted up a bit for high-toned TVs, [2] and it has also become a jazz standard. In the 1985 musical, the song occurs after Fantine has been fired, and before "Lovely Ladies". In the original French production and the 2012 film adaptation , these two musical numbers are swapped around, to place dramatic emphasis on Fantine's depressing descent into prostitution. The original French song was very extensively rewritten for the English production by Herbert Kretzmer, adding the prologue (There was a time...) and cutting the last few lines which became the ending to "Lovely Ladies" ('Don't they know they're making love to one already dead'). For the French revival in 1991, the song was loosely translated back from the English version; there are thus two very different French versions of the song. The song is typically played in the key of E-flat major with the final chorus in F major , though the pitch is shifted up a bit for high-toned TVs, [2] and it has also become a jazz standard. In the 1985 musical, the song occurs after Fantine has been fired, and before "Lovely Ladies". In the original French production and the 2012 film adaptation , these two musical numbers are swapped around, to place dramatic emphasis on Fantine's depressing descent into prostitution. The original French song was very extensively rewritten for the English production by Herbert Kretzmer, adding the prologue (There was a time...) and cutting the last few lines which became the ending to "Lovely Ladies" ('Don't they know they're making love to one already dead'). For the French revival in 1991, the song was loosely translated back from the English version; there are thus two very different French versions of the song. The English lyrics are by Neil Diamond And Herbert Kretzmer , based on the original French libretto by Alain Boublil and Jean-Marc Natel from the original French production. She thinks back to happier days and wonders at all that has gone wrong in her life. In the 1985 musical, the song occurs after Fantine has been fired, and before "Lovely Ladies". In the original French production and the 2012 film adaptation , these two musical numbers are swapped around, to place dramatic emphasis on Fantine's depressing descent into prostitution. The original French song was very extensively rewritten for the English production by Herbert Kretzmer, adding the prologue (There was a time...) and cutting the last few lines which became the ending to "Lovely Ladies" ('Don't they know they're making love to one already dead'). For the French revival in 1991, the song was loosely translated back from the English version; there are thus two very different French versions of the song. [1] It is a solo that is sung by the character Fantine during the first act. The music is by Claude-Michel Schönberg , with orchestrations by John Cameron . The English lyrics are by Neil Diamond And Herbert Kretzmer , based on the original French libretto by Alain Boublil and Jean-Marc Natel from the original French production. The song is a lament, sung by the anguished Fantine, who has just been fired from her job at the factory and thrown onto the streets. She thinks back to happier days and wonders at all that has gone wrong in her life. The song is typically played in the key of E-flat major with the final chorus in F major , though the pitch is shifted up a bit for high-toned TVs, [2] and it has also become a jazz standard. In the 1985 musical, the song occurs after Fantine has been fired, and before "Lovely Ladies". In the original French production and the 2012 film adaptation , these two musical numbers are swapped around, to place dramatic emphasis on Fantine's depressing descent into prostitution. The original French song was very extensively rewritten for the English production by Herbert Kretzmer, adding the prologue (There was a time...) and cutting the last few lines which became the ending to "Lovely Ladies" ('Don't they know they're making love to one already dead'). For the French revival in 1991, the song was loosely translated back from the English version; there are thus two very different French versions of the song. 2016) ( ) "I Dreamed a Dream" Song by Rose Laurens as Fantine from Les Misérables Language French English Published 1980 Recorded 1980 (French cast) 1985 (London cast) 1987 (Broadway cast) Genre Musical theatrical pop Composer(s) Claude-Michel Schönberg Lyricist(s) Alain Boublil (French) Herbert Kretzmer (English) " I Dreamed a Dream " is a song from the musical Les Misérables . [1] It is a solo that is sung by the character Fantine during the first act. The music is by Claude-Michel Schönberg , with orchestrations by John Cameron . The English lyrics are by Neil Diamond And Herbert Kretzmer , based on the original French libretto by Alain Boublil and Jean-Marc Natel from the original French production. The song is a lament, sung by the anguished Fantine, who has just been fired from her job at the factory and thrown onto the streets. She thinks back to happier days and wonders at all that has gone wrong in her life. The song is typically played in the key of E-flat major with the final chorus in F major , though the pitch is shifted up a bit for high-toned TVs, [2] and it has also become a jazz standard. In the 1985 musical, the song occurs after Fantine has been fired, and before "Lovely Ladies". In the original French production and the 2012 film adaptation , these two musical numbers are swapped around, to place dramatic emphasis on Fantine's depressing descent into prostitution. The original French song was very extensively rewritten for the English production by Herbert Kretzmer, adding the prologue (There was a time...) and cutting the last few lines which became the ending to "Lovely Ladies" ('Don't they know they're making love to one already dead'). For the French revival in 1991, the song was loosely translated back from the English version; there are thus two very different French versions of the song. gold_text: 2016) ( ) "I Dreamed a Dream" Song by Rose Laurens as Fantine from Les Misérables Language French English Published 1980 Recorded 1980 (French cast) 1985 (London cast) 1987 (Broadway cast) Genre Musical theatrical pop Composer(s) Claude-Michel Schönberg Lyricist(s) Alain Boublil (French) Herbert Kretzmer (English) " I Dreamed a Dream " is a song from the musical Les Misérables . [1] It is a solo that is sung by the character Fantine during the first act. The music is by Claude-Michel Schönberg , with orchestrations by John Cameron . The English lyrics are by Neil Diamond And Herbert Kretzmer , based on the original French libretto by Alain Boublil and Jean-Marc Natel from the original French production. The song is a lament, sung by the anguished Fantine, who has just been fired from her job at the factory and thrown onto the streets. She thinks back to happier days and wonders at all that has gone wrong in her life. The song is typically played in the key of E-flat major with the final chorus in F major , though the pitch is shifted up a bit for high-toned TVs, [2] and it has also become a jazz standard. In the 1985 musical, the song occurs after Fantine has been fired, and before "Lovely Ladies". In the original French production and the 2012 film adaptation , these two musical numbers are swapped around, to place dramatic emphasis on Fantine's depressing descent into prostitution. The original French song was very extensively rewritten for the English production by Herbert Kretzmer, adding the prologue (There was a time...) and cutting the last few lines which became the ending to "Lovely Ladies" ('Don't they know they're making love to one already dead'). For the French revival in 1991, the song was loosely translated back from the English version; there are thus two very different French versions of the song. 2016) ( ) "I Dreamed a Dream" Song by Rose Laurens as Fantine from Les Misérables Language French English Published 1980 Recorded 1980 (French cast) 1985 (London cast) 1987 (Broadway cast) Genre Musical theatrical pop Composer(s) Claude-Michel Schönberg Lyricist(s) Alain Boublil (French) Herbert Kretzmer (English) " I Dreamed a Dream " is a song from the musical Les Misérables . [1] It is a solo that is sung by the character Fantine during the first act. The music is by Claude-Michel Schönberg , with orchestrations by John Cameron . The English lyrics are by Neil Diamond And Herbert Kretzmer , based on the original French libretto by Alain Boublil and Jean-Marc Natel from the original French production. The song is a lament, sung by the anguished Fantine, who has just been fired from her job at the factory and thrown onto the streets. She thinks back to happier days and wonders at all that has gone wrong in her life. The song is typically played in the key of E-flat major with the final chorus in F major , though the pitch is shifted up a bit for high-toned TVs, [2] and it has also become a jazz standard. In the 1985 musical, the song occurs after Fantine has been fired, and before "Lovely Ladies". In the original French production and the 2012 film adaptation , these two musical numbers are swapped around, to place dramatic emphasis on Fantine's depressing descent into prostitution. The original French song was very extensively rewritten for the English production by Herbert Kretzmer, adding the prologue (There was a time...) and cutting the last few lines which became the ending to "Lovely Ladies" ('Don't they know they're making love to one already dead'). For the French revival in 1991, the song was loosely translated back from the English version; there are thus two very different French versions of the song. [1] It is a solo that is sung by the character Fantine during the first act. The music is by Claude-Michel Schönberg , with orchestrations by John Cameron . The English lyrics are by Neil Diamond And Herbert Kretzmer , based on the original French libretto by Alain Boublil and Jean-Marc Natel from the original French production. The song is a lament, sung by the anguished Fantine, who has just been fired from her job at the factory and thrown onto the streets. She thinks back to happier days and wonders at all that has gone wrong in her life. The song is typically played in the key of E-flat major with the final chorus in F major , though the pitch is shifted up a bit for high-toned TVs, [2] and it has also become a jazz standard. In the 1985 musical, the song occurs after Fantine has been fired, and before "Lovely Ladies". In the original French production and the 2012 film adaptation , these two musical numbers are swapped around, to place dramatic emphasis on Fantine's depressing descent into prostitution. The original French song was very extensively rewritten for the English production by Herbert Kretzmer, adding the prologue (There was a time...) and cutting the last few lines which became the ending to "Lovely Ladies" ('Don't they know they're making love to one already dead'). For the French revival in 1991, the song was loosely translated back from the English version; there are thus two very different French versions of the song. 2016) ( ) "I Dreamed a Dream" Song by Rose Laurens as Fantine from Les Misérables Language French English Published 1980 Recorded 1980 (French cast) 1985 (London cast) 1987 (Broadway cast) Genre Musical theatrical pop Composer(s) Claude-Michel Schönberg Lyricist(s) Alain Boublil (French) Herbert Kretzmer (English) " I Dreamed a Dream " is a song from the musical Les Misérables . [1] It is a solo that is sung by the character Fantine during the first act. The music is by Claude-Michel Schönberg , with orchestrations by John Cameron . The English lyrics are by Neil Diamond And Herbert Kretzmer , based on the original French libretto by Alain Boublil and Jean-Marc Natel from the original French production. The song is a lament, sung by the anguished Fantine, who has just been fired from her job at the factory and thrown onto the streets. She thinks back to happier days and wonders at all that has gone wrong in her life. The song is typically played in the key of E-flat major with the final chorus in F major , though the pitch is shifted up a bit for high-toned TVs, [2] and it has also become a jazz standard. In the 1985 musical, the song occurs after Fantine has been fired, and before "Lovely Ladies". In the original French production and the 2012 film adaptation , these two musical numbers are swapped around, to place dramatic emphasis on Fantine's depressing descent into prostitution. The original French song was very extensively rewritten for the English production by Herbert Kretzmer, adding the prologue (There was a time...) and cutting the last few lines which became the ending to "Lovely Ladies" ('Don't they know they're making love to one already dead'). For the French revival in 1991, the song was loosely translated back from the English version; there are thus two very different French versions of the song. gold_text: 2016) ( ) "I Dreamed a Dream" Song by Rose Laurens as Fantine from Les Misérables Language French English Published 1980 Recorded 1980 (French cast) 1985 (London cast) 1987 (Broadway cast) Genre Musical theatrical pop Composer(s) Claude-Michel Schönberg Lyricist(s) Alain Boublil (French) Herbert Kretzmer (English) " I Dreamed a Dream " is a song from the musical Les Misérables . [1] It is a solo that is sung by the character Fantine during the first act. The music is by Claude-Michel Schönberg , with orchestrations by John Cameron . The English lyrics are by Neil Diamond And Herbert Kretzmer , based on the original French libretto by Alain Boublil and Jean-Marc Natel from the original French production. The song is a lament, sung by the anguished Fantine, who has just been fired from her job at the factory and thrown onto the streets. She thinks back to happier days and wonders at all that has gone wrong in her life. The song is typically played in the key of E-flat major with the final chorus in F major , though the pitch is shifted up a bit for high-toned TVs, [2] and it has also become a jazz standard. In the 1985 musical, the song occurs after Fantine has been fired, and before "Lovely Ladies". In the original French production and the 2012 film adaptation , these two musical numbers are swapped around, to place dramatic emphasis on Fantine's depressing descent into prostitution. The original French song was very extensively rewritten for the English production by Herbert Kretzmer, adding the prologue (There was a time...) and cutting the last few lines which became the ending to "Lovely Ladies" ('Don't they know they're making love to one already dead'). For the French revival in 1991, the song was loosely translated back from the English version; there are thus two very different French versions of the song. The song is typically played in the key of E-flat major with the final chorus in F major , though the pitch is shifted up a bit for high-toned TVs, [2] and it has also become a jazz standard. In the 1985 musical, the song occurs after Fantine has been fired, and before "Lovely Ladies". In the original French production and the 2012 film adaptation , these two musical numbers are swapped around, to place dramatic emphasis on Fantine's depressing descent into prostitution. The original French song was very extensively rewritten for the English production by Herbert Kretzmer, adding the prologue (There was a time...) and cutting the last few lines which became the ending to "Lovely Ladies" ('Don't they know they're making love to one already dead'). For the French revival in 1991, the song was loosely translated back from the English version; there are thus two very different French versions of the song. The English lyrics are by Neil Diamond And Herbert Kretzmer , based on the original French libretto by Alain Boublil and Jean-Marc Natel from the original French production. The song is a lament, sung by the anguished Fantine, who has just been fired from her job at the factory and thrown onto the streets. She thinks back to happier days and wonders at all that has gone wrong in her life. The song is typically played in the key of E-flat major with the final chorus in F major , though the pitch is shifted up a bit for high-toned TVs, [2] and it has also become a jazz standard. In the 1985 musical, the song occurs after Fantine has been fired, and before "Lovely Ladies". In the original French production and the 2012 film adaptation , these two musical numbers are swapped around, to place dramatic emphasis on Fantine's depressing descent into prostitution. The original French song was very extensively rewritten for the English production by Herbert Kretzmer, adding the prologue (There was a time...) and cutting the last few lines which became the ending to "Lovely Ladies" ('Don't they know they're making love to one already dead'). For the French revival in 1991, the song was loosely translated back from the English version; there are thus two very different French versions of the song. model_answer: The song "I Dreamed a Dream" in Les Misérables is sung by the character Fantine during the first act. The music is by Claude-Michel Schönberg, with orchestrations by John Cameron. The English lyrics are by Neil Diamond And Herbert Kretzmer, based on the original French libretto by Alain Boublil and Jean-Marc Natel from the original French production. The song is a lament, sung by the anguished Fantine, who has just been fired from her job at the factory and thrown onto the streets. She thinks back to happier days and wonders at all that has gone wrong in her life. The song is typically played in the key of E-flat major with the final chorus in F major, though the pitch is shifted up a bit for high-toned TVs, [2] and it has also become a jazz standard. In the 1985 musical, the song occurs after Fantine has been fired, and before "Lovely Ladies". In the original French production and the 2012 film adaptation, these two musical numbers are swapped around, to place dramatic emphasis on Fantine's depressing descent into prostitution. The original French song was very extensively rewritten for the English production by Herbert Kretzmer, adding the prologue (There was a time...) and cutting the last few lines which became the ending to "Lovely Ladies" ('Don't they know they're making love to one already dead'). For the French revival in 1991, the song was loosely translated back from the English version; there are thus two very different French versions of the song.

question: who sang i dreamed a dream in les miserables
gold_text: 2016) ( ) "I Dreamed a Dream" Song by Rose Laurens as Fantine from Les Misérables Language French English Published 1980 Recorded 1980 (French cast) 1985 (London cast) 1987 (Broadway cast) Genre Musical theatrical pop Composer(s) Claude-Michel Schönberg Lyricist(s) Alain Boublil (French) Herbert Kretzmer (English) " I Dreamed a Dream " is a song from the musical Les Misérables . [1] It is a solo that is sung by the character Fantine during the first act. The music is by Claude-Michel Schönberg , with orchestrations by John Cameron . The English lyrics are by Neil Diamond And Herbert Kretzmer , based on the original French libretto by Alain Boublil and Jean-Marc Natel from the original French production. The song is a lament, sung by the anguished Fantine, who has just been fired from her job at the factory and thrown onto the streets. She thinks back to happier days and wonders at all that has gone wrong in her life. The song is typically played in the key of E-flat major with the final chorus in F major , though the pitch is shifted up a bit for high-toned TVs, [2] and it has also become a jazz standard. In the 1985 musical, the song occurs after Fantine has been fired, and before "Lovely Ladies". In the original French production and the 2012 film adaptation , these two musical numbers are swapped around, to place dramatic emphasis on Fantine's depressing descent into prostitution. The original French song was very extensively rewritten for the English production by Herbert Kretzmer, adding the prologue (There was a time...) and cutting the last few lines which became the ending to "Lovely Ladies" ('Don't they know they're making love to one already dead'). For the French revival in 1991, the song was loosely translated back from the English version; there are thus two very different French versions of the song. model_answer: The song "I Dreamed a Dream" from the musical Les Misérables was sung by Rose Laurens in the French cast of the musical. The music was composed by Claude-Michel Schönberg, with orchestrations by John Cameron. The English lyrics were written by Neil Diamond and Herbert Kretzmer, based on the original French libretto by Alain Boublil and Jean-Marc Natel from the original French production. The song is a solo that is sung by the character Fantine during the first act, and it is a lament, sung by the anguished Fantine, who has just been fired from her job at the factory and thrown onto the streets. The song is typically played in the key of E-flat major with the final chorus in F major, though the pitch is shifted up a bit for high-toned TVs. The song has also become a jazz standard. In the 1985 musical, the song occurs after Fantine has been fired, and before "Lovely Ladies". In the original French production and the 2012 film adaptation, these two musical numbers are swapped around, to place dramatic emphasis on Fantine's depressing descent into prostitution.

question: who sang i dreamed a dream in les miserables
gold_text: 2016) ( ) "I Dreamed a Dream" Song by Rose Laurens as Fantine from Les Misérables Language French English Published 1980 Recorded 1980 (French cast) 1985 (London cast) 1987 (Broadway cast) Genre Musical theatrical pop Composer(s) Claude-Michel Schönberg Lyricist(s) Alain Boublil (French) Herbert Kretzmer (English) " I Dreamed a Dream " is a song from the musical Les Misérables . [1] It is a solo that is sung by the character Fantine during the first act. The music is by Claude-Michel Schönberg , with orchestrations by John Cameron . The English lyrics are by Neil Diamond And Herbert Kretzmer , based on the original French libretto by Alain Boublil and Jean-Marc Natel from the original French production. The song is a lament, sung by the anguished Fantine, who has just been fired from her job at the factory and thrown onto the streets. She thinks back to happier days and wonders at all that has gone wrong in her life. The song is typically played in the key of E-flat major with the final chorus in F major , though the pitch is shifted up a bit for high-toned TVs, [2] and it has also become a jazz standard. In the 1985 musical, the song occurs after Fantine has been fired, and before "Lovely Ladies". In the original French production and the 2012 film adaptation , these two musical numbers are swapped around, to place dramatic emphasis on Fantine's depressing descent into prostitution. The original French song was very extensively rewritten for the English production by Herbert Kretzmer, adding the prologue (There was a time...) and cutting the last few lines which became the ending to "Lovely Ladies" ('Don't they know they're making love to one already dead'). For the French revival in 1991, the song was loosely translated back from the English version; there are thus two very different French versions of the song. model_answer: The song "I Dreamed a Dream" from the musical Les Misérables was sung by Rose Laurens in the French cast of the musical. The music was composed by Claude-Michel Schönberg, with orchestrations by John Cameron. The English lyrics were written by Neil Diamond and Herbert Kretzmer, based on the original French libretto by Alain Boublil and Jean-Marc Natel from the original French production. The song is a solo that is sung by the character Fantine during the first act, and it is a lament, sung by the anguished Fantine, who has just been fired from her job at the factory and thrown onto the streets. The song is typically played in the key of E-flat major with the final chorus in F major, though the pitch is shifted up a bit for high-toned TVs. The song has also become a jazz standard. In the 1985 musical, the song occurs after Fantine has been fired, and before "Lovely Ladies". In the original French production and the 2012 film adaptation, these two musical numbers are swapped around, to place dramatic emphasis on Fantine's depressing descent into prostitution.

The English lyrics are by Neil Diamond And Herbert Kretzmer , based on the original French libretto by Alain Boublil and Jean-Marc Natel from the original French production. In the original French production and the 2012 film adaptation , these two musical numbers are swapped around, to place dramatic emphasis on Fantine's depressing descent into prostitution. For the French revival in 1991, the song was loosely translated back from the English version; there are thus two very different French versions of the song. gold_text: 2016) ( ) "I Dreamed a Dream" Song by Rose Laurens as Fantine from Les Misérables Language French English Published 1980 Recorded 1980 (French cast) 1985 (London cast) 1987 (Broadway cast) Genre Musical theatrical pop Composer(s) Claude-Michel Schönberg Lyricist(s) Alain Boublil (French) Herbert Kretzmer (English) " I Dreamed a Dream " is a song from the musical Les Misérables . [1] It is a solo that is sung by the character Fantine during the first act. The music is by Claude-Michel Schönberg , with orchestrations by John Cameron . The English lyrics are by Neil Diamond And Herbert Kretzmer , based on the original French libretto by Alain Boublil and Jean-Marc Natel from the original French production. The song is a lament, sung by the anguished Fantine, who has just been fired from her job at the factory and thrown onto the streets. She thinks back to happier days and wonders at all that has gone wrong in her life. The song is typically played in the key of E-flat major with the final chorus in F major , though the pitch is shifted up a bit for high-toned TVs, [2] and it has also become a jazz standard. In the 1985 musical, the song occurs after Fantine has been fired, and before "Lovely Ladies". In the original French production and the 2012 film adaptation , these two musical numbers are swapped around, to place dramatic emphasis on Fantine's depressing descent into prostitution. The original French song was very extensively rewritten for the English production by Herbert Kretzmer, adding the prologue (There was a time...) and cutting the last few lines which became the ending to "Lovely Ladies" ('Don't they know they're making love to one already dead'). For the French revival in 1991, the song was loosely translated back from the English version; there are thus two very different French versions of the song. model_answer: The song "I Dreamed a Dream" in Les Misérables is sung by the character Fantine during the first act. The music is by Claude-Michel Schönberg, with orchestrations by John Cameron. The English lyrics are by Neil Diamond And Herbert Kretzmer, based on the original French libretto by Alain Boublil and Jean-Marc Natel from the original French production. The song is a lament, sung by the anguished Fantine, who has just been fired from her job at the factory and thrown onto the streets. She thinks back to happier days and wonders at all that has gone wrong in her life. The song is typically played in the key of E-flat major with the final chorus in F major, though the pitch is shifted up a bit for high-toned TVs, [2] and it has also become a jazz standard. In the 1985 musical, the song occurs after Fantine has been fired, and before "Lovely Ladies". In the original French production and the 2012 film adaptation, these two musical numbers are swapped around, to place dramatic emphasis on Fantine's depressing descent into prostitution. The original French song was very extensively rewritten for the English production by Herbert Kretzmer, adding the prologue (There was a time...) and cutting the last few lines which became the ending to "Lovely Ladies" ('Don't they know they're making love to one already dead'). For the French revival in 1991, the song was loosely translated back from the English version; there are thus two very different French versions of the song.

gold_text: 2016) ( ) "I Dreamed a Dream" Song by Rose Laurens as Fantine from Les Misérables Language French English Published 1980 Recorded 1980 (French cast) 1985 (London cast) 1987 (Broadway cast) Genre Musical theatrical pop Composer(s) Claude-Michel Schönberg Lyricist(s) Alain Boublil (French) Herbert Kretzmer (English) " I Dreamed a Dream " is a song from the musical Les Misérables . [1] It is a solo that is sung by the character Fantine during the first act. The music is by Claude-Michel Schönberg , with orchestrations by John Cameron . The English lyrics are by Neil Diamond And Herbert Kretzmer , based on the original French libretto by Alain Boublil and Jean-Marc Natel from the original French production. The song is a lament, sung by the anguished Fantine, who has just been fired from her job at the factory and thrown onto the streets. She thinks back to happier days and wonders at all that has gone wrong in her life. The song is typically played in the key of E-flat major with the final chorus in F major , though the pitch is shifted up a bit for high-toned TVs, [2] and it has also become a jazz standard. In the 1985 musical, the song occurs after Fantine has been fired, and before "Lovely Ladies". In the original French production and the 2012 film adaptation , these two musical numbers are swapped around, to place dramatic emphasis on Fantine's depressing descent into prostitution. The original French song was very extensively rewritten for the English production by Herbert Kretzmer, adding the prologue (There was a time...) and cutting the last few lines which became the ending to "Lovely Ladies" ('Don't they know they're making love to one already dead'). For the French revival in 1991, the song was loosely translated back from the English version; there are thus two very different French versions of the song. 2016) ( ) "I Dreamed a Dream" Song by Rose Laurens as Fantine from Les Misérables Language French English Published 1980 Recorded 1980 (French cast) 1985 (London cast) 1987 (Broadway cast) Genre Musical theatrical pop Composer(s) Claude-Michel Schönberg Lyricist(s) Alain Boublil (French) Herbert Kretzmer (English) " I Dreamed a Dream " is a song from the musical Les Misérables . [1] It is a solo that is sung by the character Fantine during the first act. The music is by Claude-Michel Schönberg , with orchestrations by John Cameron . The English lyrics are by Neil Diamond And Herbert Kretzmer , based on the original French libretto by Alain Boublil and Jean-Marc Natel from the original French production. The song is a lament, sung by the anguished Fantine, who has just been fired from her job at the factory and thrown onto the streets. She thinks back to happier days and wonders at all that has gone wrong in her life. The song is typically played in the key of E-flat major with the final chorus in F major , though the pitch is shifted up a bit for high-toned TVs, [2] and it has also become a jazz standard. In the 1985 musical, the song occurs after Fantine has been fired, and before "Lovely Ladies". In the original French production and the 2012 film adaptation , these two musical numbers are swapped around, to place dramatic emphasis on Fantine's depressing descent into prostitution. The original French song was very extensively rewritten for the English production by Herbert Kretzmer, adding the prologue (There was a time...) and cutting the last few lines which became the ending to "Lovely Ladies" ('Don't they know they're making love to one already dead'). For the French revival in 1991, the song was loosely translated back from the English version; there are thus two very different French versions of the song. gold_text: 2016) ( ) "I Dreamed a Dream" Song by Rose Laurens as Fantine from Les Misérables Language French English Published 1980 Recorded 1980 (French cast) 1985 (London cast) 1987 (Broadway cast) Genre Musical theatrical pop Composer(s) Claude-Michel Schönberg Lyricist(s) Alain Boublil (French) Herbert Kretzmer (English) " I Dreamed a Dream " is a song from the musical Les Misérables . [1] It is a solo that is sung by the character Fantine during the first act. The music is by Claude-Michel Schönberg , with orchestrations by John Cameron . The English lyrics are by Neil Diamond And Herbert Kretzmer , based on the original French libretto by Alain Boublil and Jean-Marc Natel from the original French production. The song is a lament, sung by the anguished Fantine, who has just been fired from her job at the factory and thrown onto the streets. She thinks back to happier days and wonders at all that has gone wrong in her life. The song is typically played in the key of E-flat major with the final chorus in F major , though the pitch is shifted up a bit for high-toned TVs, [2] and it has also become a jazz standard. In the 1985 musical, the song occurs after Fantine has been fired, and before "Lovely Ladies". In the original French production and the 2012 film adaptation , these two musical numbers are swapped around, to place dramatic emphasis on Fantine's depressing descent into prostitution. The original French song was very extensively rewritten for the English production by Herbert Kretzmer, adding the prologue (There was a time...) and cutting the last few lines which became the ending to "Lovely Ladies" ('Don't they know they're making love to one already dead'). For the French revival in 1991, the song was loosely translated back from the English version; there are thus two very different French versions of the song. (February 2017) ( ) A turlough , or turlach , is a type of disappearing lake found mostly in limestone areas of Ireland, west of the River Shannon . The name comes from the Irish tuar , meaning "dry", with the suffix -lach , meaning "a place" (in an abstract sense). The -lach suffix is often mistakenly spelled and/or thought to refer to the word loch , the Irish, Scottish Gaelic and Scots word for "lake". The landforms are found in Irish karst (exposed limestone) areas. The features are almost unique to Ireland, although there is one example in Great Britain, at Cernydd Carmel near Llandeilo . [1] [2] They are of great interest to many scientists: geomorphologists are interested in how turloughs were formed, hydrologists try to explain what makes turloughs flood, botanists study the unusual vegetation which covers the turlough floor, and zoologists study the animals associated with the turloughs. The turlough at Carran , Co. Clare , Ireland in late May 2005. (February 2017) ( ) A turlough , or turlach , is a type of disappearing lake found mostly in limestone areas of Ireland, west of the River Shannon . The name comes from the Irish tuar , meaning "dry", with the suffix -lach , meaning "a place" (in an abstract sense). The -lach suffix is often mistakenly spelled and/or thought to refer to the word loch , the Irish, Scottish Gaelic and Scots word for "lake". The landforms are found in Irish karst (exposed limestone) areas. The features are almost unique to Ireland, although there is one example in Great Britain, at Cernydd Carmel near Llandeilo . [1] [2] They are of great interest to many scientists: geomorphologists are interested in how turloughs were formed, hydrologists try to explain what makes turloughs flood, botanists study the unusual vegetation which covers the turlough floor, and zoologists study the animals associated with the turloughs. (February 2017) ( ) A turlough , or turlach , is a type of disappearing lake found mostly in limestone areas of Ireland, west of the River Shannon . The name comes from the Irish tuar , meaning "dry", with the suffix -lach , meaning "a place" (in an abstract sense). The -lach suffix is often mistakenly spelled and/or thought to refer to the word loch , the Irish, Scottish Gaelic and Scots word for "lake". The landforms are found in Irish karst (exposed limestone) areas. The features are almost unique to Ireland, although there is one example in Great Britain, at Cernydd Carmel near Llandeilo . (February 2017) ( ) A turlough , or turlach , is a type of disappearing lake found mostly in limestone areas of Ireland, west of the River Shannon . The name comes from the Irish tuar , meaning "dry", with the suffix -lach , meaning "a place" (in an abstract sense). The -lach suffix is often mistakenly spelled and/or thought to refer to the word loch , the Irish, Scottish Gaelic and Scots word for "lake". The landforms are found in Irish karst (exposed limestone) areas. The features are almost unique to Ireland, although there is one example in Great Britain, at Cernydd Carmel near Llandeilo . [1] [2] They are of great interest to many scientists: geomorphologists are interested in how turloughs were formed, hydrologists try to explain what makes turloughs flood, botanists study the unusual vegetation which covers the turlough floor, and zoologists study the animals associated with the turloughs. (February 2017) ( ) A turlough , or turlach , is a type of disappearing lake found mostly in limestone areas of Ireland, west of the River Shannon . The name comes from the Irish tuar , meaning "dry", with the suffix -lach , meaning "a place" (in an abstract sense). The -lach suffix is often mistakenly spelled and/or thought to refer to the word loch , the Irish, Scottish Gaelic and Scots word for "lake". The landforms are found in Irish karst (exposed limestone) areas. The features are almost unique to Ireland, although there is one example in Great Britain, at Cernydd Carmel near Llandeilo . [1] [2] They are of great interest to many scientists: geomorphologists are interested in how turloughs were formed, hydrologists try to explain what makes turloughs flood, botanists study the unusual vegetation which covers the turlough floor, and zoologists study the animals associated with the turloughs. The turlough at Carran , Co. Clare , Ireland in late May 2005. (February 2017) ( ) A turlough , or turlach , is a type of disappearing lake found mostly in limestone areas of Ireland, west of the River Shannon . The name comes from the Irish tuar , meaning "dry", with the suffix -lach , meaning "a place" (in an abstract sense). The -lach suffix is often mistakenly spelled and/or thought to refer to the word loch , the Irish, Scottish Gaelic and Scots word for "lake". The landforms are found in Irish karst (exposed limestone) areas. The features are almost unique to Ireland, although there is one example in Great Britain, at Cernydd Carmel near Llandeilo . [1] [2] They are of great interest to many scientists: geomorphologists are interested in how turloughs were formed, hydrologists try to explain what makes turloughs flood, botanists study the unusual vegetation which covers the turlough floor, and zoologists study the animals associated with the turloughs. (February 2017) ( ) A turlough , or turlach , is a type of disappearing lake found mostly in limestone areas of Ireland, west of the River Shannon . The name comes from the Irish tuar , meaning "dry", with the suffix -lach , meaning "a place" (in an abstract sense). The -lach suffix is often mistakenly spelled and/or thought to refer to the word loch , the Irish, Scottish Gaelic and Scots word for "lake". The landforms are found in Irish karst (exposed limestone) areas. The features are almost unique to Ireland, although there is one example in Great Britain, at Cernydd Carmel near Llandeilo . [1] [2] They are of great interest to many scientists: geomorphologists are interested in how turloughs were formed, hydrologists try to explain what makes turloughs flood, botanists study the unusual vegetation which covers the turlough floor, and zoologists study the animals associated with the turloughs. The turlough at Carran , Co. Clare , Ireland in late May 2005. (February 2017) ( ) A turlough , or turlach , is a type of disappearing lake found mostly in limestone areas of Ireland, west of the River Shannon . The name comes from the Irish tuar , meaning "dry", with the suffix -lach , meaning "a place" (in an abstract sense). The -lach suffix is often mistakenly spelled and/or thought to refer to the word loch , the Irish, Scottish Gaelic and Scots word for "lake". The landforms are found in Irish karst (exposed limestone) areas. The features are almost unique to Ireland, although there is one example in Great Britain, at Cernydd Carmel near Llandeilo . [1] [2] They are of great interest to many scientists: geomorphologists are interested in how turloughs were formed, hydrologists try to explain what makes turloughs flood, botanists study the unusual vegetation which covers the turlough floor, and zoologists study the animals associated with the turloughs. (February 2017) ( ) A turlough , or turlach , is a type of disappearing lake found mostly in limestone areas of Ireland, west of the River Shannon . The name comes from the Irish tuar , meaning "dry", with the suffix -lach , meaning "a place" (in an abstract sense). The -lach suffix is often mistakenly spelled and/or thought to refer to the word loch , the Irish, Scottish Gaelic and Scots word for "lake". The landforms are found in Irish karst (exposed limestone) areas. The features are almost unique to Ireland, although there is one example in Great Britain, at Cernydd Carmel near Llandeilo . [1] [2] They are of great interest to many scientists: geomorphologists are interested in how turloughs were formed, hydrologists try to explain what makes turloughs flood, botanists study the unusual vegetation which covers the turlough floor, and zoologists study the animals associated with the turloughs. The turlough at Carran , Co. Clare , Ireland in late May 2005. (February 2017) ( ) A turlough , or turlach , is a type of disappearing lake found mostly in limestone areas of Ireland, west of the River Shannon . The name comes from the Irish tuar , meaning "dry", with the suffix -lach , meaning "a place" (in an abstract sense). The -lach suffix is often mistakenly spelled and/or thought to refer to the word loch , the Irish, Scottish Gaelic and Scots word for "lake". The landforms are found in Irish karst (exposed limestone) areas. The features are almost unique to Ireland, although there is one example in Great Britain, at Cernydd Carmel near Llandeilo . [1] [2] They are of great interest to many scientists: geomorphologists are interested in how turloughs were formed, hydrologists try to explain what makes turloughs flood, botanists study the unusual vegetation which covers the turlough floor, and zoologists study the animals associated with the turloughs. (February 2017) ( ) A turlough , or turlach , is a type of disappearing lake found mostly in limestone areas of Ireland, west of the River Shannon . The name comes from the Irish tuar , meaning "dry", with the suffix -lach , meaning "a place" (in an abstract sense). The -lach suffix is often mistakenly spelled and/or thought to refer to the word loch , the Irish, Scottish Gaelic and Scots word for "lake". The landforms are found in Irish karst (exposed limestone) areas. The features are almost unique to Ireland, although there is one example in Great Britain, at Cernydd Carmel near Llandeilo . [1] [2] They are of great interest to many scientists: geomorphologists are interested in how turloughs were formed, hydrologists try to explain what makes turloughs flood, botanists study the unusual vegetation which covers the turlough floor, and zoologists study the animals associated with the turloughs. The turlough at Carran , Co. Clare , Ireland in late May 2005. (February 2017) ( ) A turlough , or turlach , is a type of disappearing lake found mostly in limestone areas of Ireland, west of the River Shannon . The name comes from the Irish tuar , meaning "dry", with the suffix -lach , meaning "a place" (in an abstract sense). The -lach suffix is often mistakenly spelled and/or thought to refer to the word loch , the Irish, Scottish Gaelic and Scots word for "lake". The landforms are found in Irish karst (exposed limestone) areas. The features are almost unique to Ireland, although there is one example in Great Britain, at Cernydd Carmel near Llandeilo . (February 2017) ( ) A turlough , or turlach , is a type of disappearing lake found mostly in limestone areas of Ireland, west of the River Shannon . The name comes from the Irish tuar , meaning "dry", with the suffix -lach , meaning "a place" (in an abstract sense). The -lach suffix is often mistakenly spelled and/or thought to refer to the word loch , the Irish, Scottish Gaelic and Scots word for "lake". The landforms are found in Irish karst (exposed limestone) areas. The features are almost unique to Ireland, although there is one example in Great Britain, at Cernydd Carmel near Llandeilo . [1] [2] They are of great interest to many scientists: geomorphologists are interested in how turloughs were formed, hydrologists try to explain what makes turloughs flood, botanists study the unusual vegetation which covers the turlough floor, and zoologists study the animals associated with the turloughs. The turlough at Carran , Co. Clare , Ireland in late May 2005. Turloughs are of great interest to scientists, including geomorphologists, hydrologists, botanists, and zoologists, who study the unique plant and animal life found in these areas. The water level in turloughs can fluctuate significantly, with the highest levels occurring during periods of heavy rainfall.

(February 2017) ( ) A turlough , or turlach , is a type of disappearing lake found mostly in limestone areas of Ireland, west of the River Shannon . The name comes from the Irish tuar , meaning "dry", with the suffix -lach , meaning "a place" (in an abstract sense). The -lach suffix is often mistakenly spelled and/or thought to refer to the word loch , the Irish, Scottish Gaelic and Scots word for "lake". The landforms are found in Irish karst (exposed limestone) areas. The features are almost unique to Ireland, although there is one example in Great Britain, at Cernydd Carmel near Llandeilo . (February 2017) ( ) A turlough , or turlach , is a type of disappearing lake found mostly in limestone areas of Ireland, west of the River Shannon . The name comes from the Irish tuar , meaning "dry", with the suffix -lach , meaning "a place" (in an abstract sense). The -lach suffix is often mistakenly spelled and/or thought to refer to the word loch , the Irish, Scottish Gaelic and Scots word for "lake". The landforms are found in Irish karst (exposed limestone) areas. The features are almost unique to Ireland, although there is one example in Great Britain, at Cernydd Carmel near Llandeilo . [1] [2] They are of great interest to many scientists: geomorphologists are interested in how turloughs were formed, hydrologists try to explain what makes turloughs flood, botanists study the unusual vegetation which covers the turlough floor, and zoologists study the animals associated with the turloughs. The turlough at Carran , Co. Clare , Ireland in late May 2005. model_answer: The type of disappearing lake found in limestone areas in the west of Ireland is called a turlough (or turlach). Turloughs are seasonal pools that form in karst areas, which are regions where the solubility of limestone has led to the formation of underground drainage systems, sinkholes, and caves. These lakes are typically found in counties Galway, Clare, Mayo, and Roscommon, with only a few examples in other parts of Ireland and Great Britain. Turloughs are of interest to scientists studying geomorphology, hydrology, botany, and zoology, as they provide unique habitats for plants and animals. The formation of turloughs is influenced by factors such as rainfall, temperature, and the geology of the area.

(February 2017) ( ) A turlough , or turlach , is a type of disappearing lake found mostly in limestone areas of Ireland, west of the River Shannon . The name comes from the Irish tuar , meaning "dry", with the suffix -lach , meaning "a place" (in an abstract sense). The -lach suffix is often mistakenly spelled and/or thought to refer to the word loch , the Irish, Scottish Gaelic and Scots word for "lake". The landforms are found in Irish karst (exposed limestone) areas. The features are almost unique to Ireland, although there is one example in Great Britain, at Cernydd Carmel near Llandeilo . [1] [2] They are of great interest to many scientists: geomorphologists are interested in how turloughs were formed, hydrologists try to explain what makes turloughs flood, botanists study the unusual vegetation which covers the turlough floor, and zoologists study the animals associated with the turloughs. (February 2017) ( ) A turlough , or turlach , is a type of disappearing lake found mostly in limestone areas of Ireland, west of the River Shannon . The name comes from the Irish tuar , meaning "dry", with the suffix -lach , meaning "a place" (in an abstract sense). The -lach suffix is often mistakenly spelled and/or thought to refer to the word loch , the Irish, Scottish Gaelic and Scots word for "lake". The landforms are found in Irish karst (exposed limestone) areas. The features are almost unique to Ireland, although there is one example in Great Britain, at Cernydd Carmel near Llandeilo . [1] [2] They are of great interest to many scientists: geomorphologists are interested in how turloughs were formed, hydrologists try to explain what makes turloughs flood, botanists study the unusual vegetation which covers the turlough floor, and zoologists study the animals associated with the turloughs. The turlough at Carran , Co. Clare , Ireland in late May 2005. (February 2017) ( ) A turlough , or turlach , is a type of disappearing lake found mostly in limestone areas of Ireland, west of the River Shannon . The name comes from the Irish tuar , meaning "dry", with the suffix -lach , meaning "a place" (in an abstract sense). The -lach suffix is often mistakenly spelled and/or thought to refer to the word loch , the Irish, Scottish Gaelic and Scots word for "lake". The landforms are found in Irish karst (exposed limestone) areas. The features are almost unique to Ireland, although there is one example in Great Britain, at Cernydd Carmel near Llandeilo . [1] [2] They are of great interest to many scientists: geomorphologists are interested in how turloughs were formed, hydrologists try to explain what makes turloughs flood, botanists study the unusual vegetation which covers the turlough floor, and zoologists study the animals associated with the turloughs. (February 2017) ( ) A turlough , or turlach , is a type of disappearing lake found mostly in limestone areas of Ireland, west of the River Shannon . The name comes from the Irish tuar , meaning "dry", with the suffix -lach , meaning "a place" (in an abstract sense). The -lach suffix is often mistakenly spelled and/or thought to refer to the word loch , the Irish, Scottish Gaelic and Scots word for "lake". The landforms are found in Irish karst (exposed limestone) areas. The features are almost unique to Ireland, although there is one example in Great Britain, at Cernydd Carmel near Llandeilo . [1] [2] They are of great interest to many scientists: geomorphologists are interested in how turloughs were formed, hydrologists try to explain what makes turloughs flood, botanists study the unusual vegetation which covers the turlough floor, and zoologists study the animals associated with the turloughs. The turlough at Carran , Co. Clare , Ireland in late May 2005. The name comes from the Irish tuar , meaning "dry", with the suffix -lach , meaning "a place" (in an abstract sense). The -lach suffix is often mistakenly spelled and/or thought to refer to the word loch , the Irish, Scottish Gaelic and Scots word for "lake". (February 2017) ( ) A turlough , or turlach , is a type of disappearing lake found mostly in limestone areas of Ireland, west of the River Shannon . The name comes from the Irish tuar , meaning "dry", with the suffix -lach , meaning "a place" (in an abstract sense). The -lach suffix is often mistakenly spelled and/or thought to refer to the word loch , the Irish, Scottish Gaelic and Scots word for "lake". The landforms are found in Irish karst (exposed limestone) areas. The features are almost unique to Ireland, although there is one example in Great Britain, at Cernydd Carmel near Llandeilo . (February 2017) ( ) A turlough , or turlach , is a type of disappearing lake found mostly in limestone areas of Ireland, west of the River Shannon . The name comes from the Irish tuar , meaning "dry", with the suffix -lach , meaning "a place" (in an abstract sense). The -lach suffix is often mistakenly spelled and/or thought to refer to the word loch , the Irish, Scottish Gaelic and Scots word for "lake". The landforms are found in Irish karst (exposed limestone) areas. The features are almost unique to Ireland, although there is one example in Great Britain, at Cernydd Carmel near Llandeilo . [1] [2] They are of great interest to many scientists: geomorphologists are interested in how turloughs were formed, hydrologists try to explain what makes turloughs flood, botanists study the unusual vegetation which covers the turlough floor, and zoologists study the animals associated with the turloughs. The turlough at Carran , Co. Clare , Ireland in late May 2005. model_answer: The type of disappearing lake found in limestone areas in the west of Ireland is called a turlough (or turlach). Turloughs are seasonal pools that form in karst areas, which are regions with soluble rock, such as limestone, dolomite, or gypsum. These lakes are typically found in counties Galway, Clare, Mayo, and Roscommon, but there are also a few examples in other parts of Ireland and even in Great Britain. Turloughs are of interest to scientists studying geomorphology, hydrology, botany, and zoology. The formation of turloughs is thought to be due to the dissolution of rock, which creates underground drainage systems, and the accumulation of water in depressions in the rock. The unique vegetation and animal life found in turloughs is also of interest to scientists. Turloughs are also known for their cultural significance in Irish mythology and folklore.

(February 2017) ( ) A turlough , or turlach , is a type of disappearing lake found mostly in limestone areas of Ireland, west of the River Shannon . The name comes from the Irish tuar , meaning "dry", with the suffix -lach , meaning "a place" (in an abstract sense). The -lach suffix is often mistakenly spelled and/or thought to refer to the word loch , the Irish, Scottish Gaelic and Scots word for "lake". The landforms are found in Irish karst (exposed limestone) areas. The features are almost unique to Ireland, although there is one example in Great Britain, at Cernydd Carmel near Llandeilo . (February 2017) ( ) A turlough , or turlach , is a type of disappearing lake found mostly in limestone areas of Ireland, west of the River Shannon . The name comes from the Irish tuar , meaning "dry", with the suffix -lach , meaning "a place" (in an abstract sense). The -lach suffix is often mistakenly spelled and/or thought to refer to the word loch , the Irish, Scottish Gaelic and Scots word for "lake". The landforms are found in Irish karst (exposed limestone) areas. The features are almost unique to Ireland, although there is one example in Great Britain, at Cernydd Carmel near Llandeilo . [1] [2] They are of great interest to many scientists: geomorphologists are interested in how turloughs were formed, hydrologists try to explain what makes turloughs flood, botanists study the unusual vegetation which covers the turlough floor, and zoologists study the animals associated with the turloughs. The turlough at Carran , Co. Clare , Ireland in late May 2005. model_answer: The type of disappearing lake found in limestone areas in the west of Ireland is called a turlough (or turlach). Turloughs are seasonal pools that form in karst areas due to the dissolution of limestone by slightly acidic rainwater. They are unique to Ireland and are of great interest to scientists studying geomorphology, hydrology, botany, and zoology. Turloughs are typically found in counties Galway, Clare, Mayo, and Roscommon, with a few examples in other counties as well. They are formed by the dissolution of limestone, which creates underground drainage systems, and the accumulation of water in depressions in the landscape. The water level in turloughs can fluctuate significantly, with some drying up completely during dry periods and others remaining wet year-round. The unique vegetation and animal life found in turloughs is also of interest to scientists, as it is adapted to the highly variable water conditions.

(February 2017) ( ) A turlough , or turlach , is a type of disappearing lake found mostly in limestone areas of Ireland, west of the River Shannon . The name comes from the Irish tuar , meaning "dry", with the suffix -lach , meaning "a place" (in an abstract sense). The -lach suffix is often mistakenly spelled and/or thought to refer to the word loch , the Irish, Scottish Gaelic and Scots word for "lake". The landforms are found in Irish karst (exposed limestone) areas. The features are almost unique to Ireland, although there is one example in Great Britain, at Cernydd Carmel near Llandeilo .
