(February 2017) ( ) A turlough , or turlach , is a type of disappearing lake found mostly in limestone areas of Ireland, west of the River Shannon . The name comes from the Irish tuar , meaning "dry", with the suffix -lach , meaning "a place" (in an abstract sense). The -lach suffix is often mistakenly spelled and/or thought to refer to the word loch , the Irish, Scottish Gaelic and Scots word for "lake". The landforms are found in Irish karst (exposed limestone) areas. The features are almost unique to Ireland, although there is one example in Great Britain, at Cernydd Carmel near Llandeilo . [1] [2] They are of great interest to many scientists: geomorphologists are interested in how turloughs were formed, hydrologists try to explain what makes turloughs flood, botanists study the unusual vegetation which covers the turlough floor, and zoologists study the animals associated with the turloughs. The turlough at Carran , Co. Clare , Ireland in late May 2005. model_answer: The type of disappearing lake found in limestone areas in the west of Ireland is called a turlough (or turlach). Turloughs are seasonal pools that form in karst areas due to the dissolution of limestone by slightly acidic rainwater. They are unique to Ireland and are of great interest to scientists studying geomorphology, hydrology, botany, and zoology. Turloughs are typically found in counties Galway, Clare, Mayo, and Roscommon, with a few examples in other counties as well. They are formed by the dissolution of limestone, which creates underground drainage systems, and the accumulation of water in depressions in the landscape. The water level in turloughs can fluctuate significantly, and they can dry up completely during dry periods. The unique vegetation and animal life found in turloughs is also of interest to scientists, as it is adapted to the highly variable water conditions.

(February 2017) ( ) A turlough , or turlach , is a type of disappearing lake found mostly in limestone areas of Ireland, west of the River Shannon . The name comes from the Irish tuar , meaning "dry", with the suffix -lach , meaning "a place" (in an abstract sense). The -lach suffix is often mistakenly spelled and/or thought to refer to the word loch , the Irish, Scottish Gaelic and Scots word for "lake". The landforms are found in Irish karst (exposed limestone) areas. The features are almost unique to Ireland, although there is one example in Great Britain, at Cernydd Carmel near Llandeilo . [1] [2] They are of great interest to many scientists: geomorphologists are interested in how turloughs were formed, hydrologists try to explain what makes turloughs flood, botanists study the unusual vegetation which covers the turlough floor, and zoologists study the animals associated with the turloughs. (February 2017) ( ) A turlough , or turlach , is a type of disappearing lake found mostly in limestone areas of Ireland, west of the River Shannon . The name comes from the Irish tuar , meaning "dry", with the suffix -lach , meaning "a place" (in an abstract sense). The -lach suffix is often mistakenly spelled and/or thought to refer to the word loch , the Irish, Scottish Gaelic and Scots word for "lake". The landforms are found in Irish karst (exposed limestone) areas. The features are almost unique to Ireland, although there is one example in Great Britain, at Cernydd Carmel near Llandeilo . [1] [2] They are of great interest to many scientists: geomorphologists are interested in how turloughs were formed, hydrologists try to explain what makes turloughs flood, botanists study the unusual vegetation which covers the turlough floor, and zoologists study the animals associated with the turloughs. The turlough at Carran , Co. Clare , Ireland in late May 2005. (February 2017) ( ) A turlough , or turlach , is a type of disappearing lake found mostly in limestone areas of Ireland, west of the River Shannon . The name comes from the Irish tuar , meaning "dry", with the suffix -lach , meaning "a place" (in an abstract sense). The -lach suffix is often mistakenly spelled and/or thought to refer to the word loch , the Irish, Scottish Gaelic and Scots word for "lake". The landforms are found in Irish karst (exposed limestone) areas. The features are almost unique to Ireland, although there is one example in Great Britain, at Cernydd Carmel near Llandeilo . (February 2017) ( ) A turlough , or turlach , is a type of disappearing lake found mostly in limestone areas of Ireland, west of the River Shannon . The name comes from the Irish tuar , meaning "dry", with the suffix -lach , meaning "a place" (in an abstract sense). The -lach suffix is often mistakenly spelled and/or thought to refer to the word loch , the Irish, Scottish Gaelic and Scots word for "lake". The landforms are found in Irish karst (exposed limestone) areas. The features are almost unique to Ireland, although there is one example in Great Britain, at Cernydd Carmel near Llandeilo . [1] [2] They are of great interest to many scientists: geomorphologists are interested in how turloughs were formed, hydrologists try to explain what makes turloughs flood, botanists study the unusual vegetation which covers the turlough floor, and zoologists study the animals associated with the turloughs. The turlough at Carran , Co. Clare , Ireland in late May 2005. (February 2017) ( ) A turlough , or turlach , is a type of disappearing lake found mostly in limestone areas of Ireland, west of the River Shannon . The name comes from the Irish tuar , meaning "dry", with the suffix -lach , meaning "a place" (in an abstract sense). The -lach suffix is often mistakenly spelled and/or thought to refer to the word loch , the Irish, Scottish Gaelic and Scots word for "lake". The landforms are found in Irish karst (exposed limestone) areas. The features are almost unique to Ireland, although there is one example in Great Britain, at Cernydd Carmel near Llandeilo . [1] [2] They are of great interest to many scientists: geomorphologists are interested in how turloughs were formed, hydrologists try to explain what makes turloughs flood, botanists study the unusual vegetation which covers the turlough floor, and zoologists study the animals associated with the turloughs. (February 2017) ( ) A turlough , or turlach , is a type of disappearing lake found mostly in limestone areas of Ireland, west of the River Shannon . The name comes from the Irish tuar , meaning "dry", with the suffix -lach , meaning "a place" (in an abstract sense). The -lach suffix is often mistakenly spelled and/or thought to refer to the word loch , the Irish, Scottish Gaelic and Scots word for "lake". The landforms are found in Irish karst (exposed limestone) areas. The features are almost unique to Ireland, although there is one example in Great Britain, at Cernydd Carmel near Llandeilo . [1] [2] They are of great interest to many scientists: geomorphologists are interested in how turloughs were formed, hydrologists try to explain what makes turloughs flood, botanists study the unusual vegetation which covers the turlough floor, and zoologists study the animals associated with the turloughs. The turlough at Carran , Co. Clare , Ireland in late May 2005. (February 2017) ( ) A turlough , or turlach , is a type of disappearing lake found mostly in limestone areas of Ireland, west of the River Shannon . The name comes from the Irish tuar , meaning "dry", with the suffix -lach , meaning "a place" (in an abstract sense). The -lach suffix is often mistakenly spelled and/or thought to refer to the word loch , the Irish, Scottish Gaelic and Scots word for "lake". The landforms are found in Irish karst (exposed limestone) areas. The features are almost unique to Ireland, although there is one example in Great Britain, at Cernydd Carmel near Llandeilo . [1] [2] They are of great interest to many scientists: geomorphologists are interested in how turloughs were formed, hydrologists try to explain what makes turloughs flood, botanists study the unusual vegetation which covers the turlough floor, and zoologists study the animals associated with the turloughs. (February 2017) ( ) A turlough , or turlach , is a type of disappearing lake found mostly in limestone areas of Ireland, west of the River Shannon . The name comes from the Irish tuar , meaning "dry", with the suffix -lach , meaning "a place" (in an abstract sense). The -lach suffix is often mistakenly spelled and/or thought to refer to the word loch , the Irish, Scottish Gaelic and Scots word for "lake". The landforms are found in Irish karst (exposed limestone) areas. The features are almost unique to Ireland, although there is one example in Great Britain, at Cernydd Carmel near Llandeilo . [1] [2] They are of great interest to many scientists: geomorphologists are interested in how turloughs were formed, hydrologists try to explain what makes turloughs flood, botanists study the unusual vegetation which covers the turlough floor, and zoologists study the animals associated with the turloughs. The turlough at Carran , Co. Clare , Ireland in late May 2005. question: when was coffee first made into a drink
gold_text: in the middle of the 15th century, in Yemen 's Sufi monasteries. [1] Coffee beans were first exported from Ethiopia to Yemen . Yemeni traders brought coffee back to their homeland and began to cultivate the bean. [13] The word qahwa originally meant wine, and Sufis in Yemen used the beverage as an aid to concentration and as a kind of spiritual intoxication when they chanted the name of God. [14] Sufis used it to keep themselves alert during their nighttime devotions. A translation of Al-Jaziri's manuscript [15] traces the spread of coffee from Arabia Felix (the present day Yemen) northward to Mecca and Medina , and then to the larger cities of Cairo , Damascus , Baghdad , and Constantinople . By 1414, the beverage was known in Mecca, and in the early 1500s was spreading to the Mameluke Sultanate of Egypt and North Africa from the Yemeni port of Mocha . [8] [14] Associated with Sufism , a myriad of coffee houses grew up in Cairo (Egypt) around the religious University of the Azhar. These coffee houses also opened in Syria, especially in the cosmopolitan city of Aleppo, [14] and then in Istanbul, the capital of the Ottoman Empire , in 1554. [14] In 1511, it was forbidden for its stimulating effect by conservative, orthodox imams at a theological court in Mecca . [16] However, these bans were to be overturned in 1524 by an order of the Ottoman Turkish Sultan Suleiman I , with Grand Mufti Mehmet Ebussuud el-İmadi issuing a fatwa allowing the consumption of coffee. [17] In Cairo , Egypt, a similar ban was instituted in 1532, and the coffeehouses and warehouses containing coffee beans were sacked. [18] During the 16th century, it had already reached the rest of the Middle East, the Safavid Empire and the Ottoman Empire . From the Middle East, coffee drinking spread to Italy, then to the rest of Europe, and coffee plants were transported by the Dutch to the East Indies and to the Americas. [2] Similarly, coffee was banned by the Ethiopian Orthodox Church some time before the 18th century. [19]

in the middle of the 15th century, in Yemen 's Sufi monasteries. [1] Coffee beans were first exported from Ethiopia to Yemen . question: when was coffee first made into a drink
gold_text: in the middle of the 15th century, in Yemen 's Sufi monasteries. [1] Coffee beans were first exported from Ethiopia to Yemen . Yemeni traders brought coffee back to their homeland and began to cultivate the bean. [13] The word qahwa originally meant wine, and Sufis in Yemen used the beverage as an aid to concentration and as a kind of spiritual intoxication when they chanted the name of God. [14] Sufis used it to keep themselves alert during their nighttime devotions. A translation of Al-Jaziri's manuscript [15] traces the spread of coffee from Arabia Felix (the present day Yemen) northward to Mecca and Medina , and then to the larger cities of Cairo , Damascus , Baghdad , and Constantinople . By 1414, the beverage was known in Mecca, and in the early 1500s was spreading to the Mameluke Sultanate of Egypt and North Africa from the Yemeni port of Mocha . [8] [14] Associated with Sufism , a myriad of coffee houses grew up in Cairo (Egypt) around the religious University of the Azhar. These coffee houses also opened in Syria, especially in the cosmopolitan city of Aleppo, [14] and then in Istanbul, the capital of the Ottoman Empire , in 1554. [14] In 1511, it was forbidden for its stimulating effect by conservative, orthodox imams at a theological court in Mecca . [16] However, these bans were to be overturned in 1524 by an order of the Ottoman Turkish Sultan Suleiman I , with Grand Mufti Mehmet Ebussuud el-İmadi issuing a fatwa allowing the consumption of coffee. [17] In Cairo , Egypt, a similar ban was instituted in 1532, and the coffeehouses and warehouses containing coffee beans were sacked. [18] During the 16th century, it had already reached the rest of the Middle East, the Safavid Empire and the Ottoman Empire . From the Middle East, coffee drinking spread to Italy, then to the rest of Europe, and coffee plants were transported by the Dutch to the East Indies and to the Americas. [2] Similarly, coffee was banned by the Ethiopian Orthodox Church some time before the 18th century. [19]

question: when was coffee first made into a drink
gold_text: in the middle of the 15th century, in Yemen 's Sufi monasteries. [1] Coffee beans were first exported from Ethiopia to Yemen . Yemeni traders brought coffee back to their homeland and began to cultivate the bean. [13] The word qahwa originally meant wine, and Sufis in Yemen used the beverage as an aid to concentration and as a kind of spiritual intoxication when they chanted the name of God. [14] Sufis used it to keep themselves alert during their nighttime devotions. A translation of Al-Jaziri's manuscript [15] traces the spread of coffee from Arabia Felix (the present day Yemen) northward to Mecca and Medina , and then to the larger cities of Cairo , Damascus , Baghdad , and Constantinople . By 1414, the beverage was known in Mecca, and in the early 1500s was spreading to the Mameluke Sultanate of Egypt and North Africa from the Yemeni port of Mocha . [8] [14] Associated with Sufism , a myriad of coffee houses grew up in Cairo (Egypt) around the religious University of the Azhar. These coffee houses also opened in Syria, especially in the cosmopolitan city of Aleppo, [14] and then in Istanbul, the capital of the Ottoman Empire , in 1554. [14] In 1511, it was forbidden for its stimulating effect by conservative, orthodox imams at a theological court in Mecca . [16] However, these bans were to be overturned in 1524 by an order of the Ottoman Turkish Sultan Suleiman I , with Grand Mufti Mehmet Ebussuud el-İmadi issuing a fatwa allowing the consumption of coffee. [17] In Cairo , Egypt, a similar ban was instituted in 1532, and the coffeehouses and warehouses containing coffee beans were sacked. [18] During the 16th century, it had already reached the rest of the Middle East, the Safavid Empire and the Ottoman Empire . From the Middle East, coffee drinking spread to Italy, then to the rest of Europe, and coffee plants were transported by the Dutch to the East Indies and to the Americas. [2] Similarly, coffee was banned by the Ethiopian Orthodox Church some time before the 18th century. [19]

question: when was coffee first made into a drink
gold_text: in the middle of the 15th century, in Yemen 's Sufi monasteries. [1] Coffee beans were first exported from Ethiopia to Yemen . Yemeni traders brought coffee back to their homeland and began to cultivate the bean. [13] The word qahwa originally meant wine, and Sufis in Yemen used the beverage as an aid to concentration and as a kind of spiritual intoxication when they chanted the name of God. [14] Sufis used it to keep themselves alert during their nighttime devotions. A translation of Al-Jaziri's manuscript [15] traces the spread of coffee from Arabia Felix (the present day Yemen) northward to Mecca and Medina , and then to the larger cities of Cairo , Damascus , Baghdad , and Constantinople . By 1414, the beverage was known in Mecca, and in the early 1500s was spreading to the Mameluke Sultanate of Egypt and North Africa from the Yemeni port of Mocha . [8] [14] Associated with Sufism , a myriad of coffee houses grew up in Cairo (Egypt) around the religious University of the Azhar. These coffee houses also opened in Syria, especially in the cosmopolitan city of Aleppo, [14] and then in Istanbul, the capital of the Ottoman Empire , in 1554. [14] In 1511, it was forbidden for its stimulating effect by conservative, orthodox imams at a theological court in Mecca . [16] However, these bans were to be overturned in 1524 by an order of the Ottoman Turkish Sultan Suleiman I , with Grand Mufti Mehmet Ebussuud el-İmadi issuing a fatwa allowing the consumption of coffee. [17] In Cairo , Egypt, a similar ban was instituted in 1532, and the coffeehouses and warehouses containing coffee beans were sacked. [18] During the 16th century, it had already reached the rest of the Middle East, the Safavid Empire and the Ottoman Empire . From the Middle East, coffee drinking spread to Italy, then to the rest of Europe, and coffee plants were transported by the Dutch to the East Indies and to the Americas. [2] Similarly, coffee was banned by the Ethiopian Orthodox Church some time before the 18th century. [19]

[13] The word qahwa originally meant wine, and Sufis in Yemen used the beverage as an aid to concentration and as a kind of spiritual intoxication when they chanted the name of God. [14] Sufis used it to keep themselves alert during their nighttime devotions. A translation of Al-Jaziri's manuscript [15] traces the spread of coffee from Arabia Felix (the present day Yemen) northward to Mecca and Medina , and then to the larger cities of Cairo , Damascus , Baghdad , and Constantinople . By 1414, the beverage was known in Mecca, and in the early 1500s was spreading to the Mameluke Sultanate of Egypt and North Africa from the Yemeni port of Mocha . [8] [14] Associated with Sufism , a myriad of coffee houses grew up in Cairo (Egypt) around the religious University of the Azhar. These coffee houses also opened in Syria, especially in the cosmopolitan city of Aleppo, [14] and then in Istanbul, the capital of the Ottoman Empire , in 1554. [14] In 1511, it was forbidden for its stimulating effect by conservative, orthodox imams at a theological court in Mecca . [16] However, these bans were to be overturned in 1524 by an order of the Ottoman Turkish Sultan Suleiman I , with Grand Mufti Mehmet Ebussuud el-İmadi issuing a fatwa allowing the consumption of coffee. [17] In Cairo , Egypt, a similar ban was instituted in 1532, and the coffeehouses and warehouses containing coffee beans were sacked. [18] During the 16th century, it had already reached the rest of the Middle East, the Safavid Empire and the Ottoman Empire . From the Middle East, coffee drinking spread to Italy, then to the rest of Europe, and coffee plants were transported by the Dutch to the East Indies and to the Americas. [2] Similarly, coffee was banned by the Ethiopian Orthodox Church some time before the 18th century. [19]

question: when was coffee first made into a drink
gold_text: in the middle of the 15th century, in Yemen 's Sufi monasteries. [1] Coffee beans were first exported from Ethiopia to Yemen . Yemeni traders brought coffee back to their homeland and began to cultivate the bean. [13] The word qahwa originally meant wine, and Sufis in Yemen used the beverage as an aid to concentration and as a kind of spiritual intoxication when they chanted the name of God. [14] Sufis used it to keep themselves alert during their nighttime devotions. A translation of Al-Jaziri's manuscript [15] traces the spread of coffee from Arabia Felix (the present day Yemen) northward to Mecca and Medina , and then to the larger cities of Cairo , Damascus , Baghdad , and Constantinople . By 1414, the beverage was known in Mecca, and in the early 1500s was spreading to the Mameluke Sultanate of Egypt and North Africa from the Yemeni port of Mocha . [8] [14] Associated with Sufism , a myriad of coffee houses grew up in Cairo (Egypt) around the religious University of the Azhar. These coffee houses also opened in Syria, especially in the cosmopolitan city of Aleppo, [14] and then in Istanbul, the capital of the Ottoman Empire , in 1554. [14] In 1511, it was forbidden for its stimulating effect by conservative, orthodox imams at a theological court in Mecca . [16] However, these bans were to be overturned in 1524 by an order of the Ottoman Turkish Sultan Suleiman I , with Grand Mufti Mehmet Ebussuud el-İmadi issuing a fatwa allowing the consumption of coffee. [17] In Cairo , Egypt, a similar ban was instituted in 1532, and the coffeehouses and warehouses containing coffee beans were sacked. [18] During the 16th century, it had already reached the rest of the Middle East, the Safavid Empire and the Ottoman Empire . From the Middle East, coffee drinking spread to Italy, then to the rest of Europe, and coffee plants were transported by the Dutch to the East Indies and to the Americas. [2] Similarly, coffee was banned by the Ethiopian Orthodox Church some time before the 18th century. [19]

However, it is important to note that coffee beans were first exported from Ethiopia to Yemen, where they were used for medicinal purposes and later as a stimulant. Sufis used it to keep themselves alert during their nighttime devotions.

Coffee houses grew up in Cairo, Egypt around the religious University of the Azhar, and then spread to other parts of the Middle East, the Safavid Empire, and the Ottoman Empire. Coffee houses and warehouses containing coffee beans were sacked in Cairo in 1532, and in 1511, it was forbidden for its stimulating effect by conservative, orthodox imams at a theological court in Mecca. However, these bans were to be overturned in 1524 by an order of the Ottoman Turkish Sultan Suleiman I, with Grand Mufti Mehmet Ebussuud el-İmadi issuing a fatwa allowing the consumption of coffee.

In 16th century, it had already reached the rest of the Middle East, the Safavid Empire and the Ottoman Empire. Yemeni traders brought coffee back to their homeland and began to cultivate the bean. [14] Sufis used it to keep themselves alert during their nighttime devotions. A translation of Al-Jaziri's manuscript [15] traces the spread of coffee from Arabia Felix (the present day Yemen) northward to Mecca and Medina , and then to the larger cities of Cairo , Damascus , Baghdad , and Constantinople . By 1414, the beverage was known in Mecca, and in the early 1500s was spreading to the Mameluke Sultanate of Egypt and North Africa from the Yemeni port of Mocha . [8] [14] Associated with Sufism , a myriad of coffee houses grew up in Cairo (Egypt) around the religious University of the Azhar. These coffee houses also opened in Syria, especially in the cosmopolitan city of Aleppo, [14] and then in Istanbul, the capital of the Ottoman Empire , in 1554. [14] In 1511, it was forbidden for its stimulating effect by conservative, orthodox imams at a theological court in Mecca . [16] However, these bans were to be overturned in 1524 by an order of the Ottoman Turkish Sultan Suleiman I , with Grand Mufti Mehmet Ebussuud el-İmadi issuing a fatwa allowing the consumption of coffee. [17] In Cairo , Egypt, a similar ban was instituted in 1532, and the coffeehouses and warehouses containing coffee beans were sacked. [18] During the 16th century, it had already reached the rest of the Middle East, the Safavid Empire and the Ottoman Empire . From the Middle East, coffee drinking spread to Italy, then to the rest of Europe, and coffee plants were transported by the Dutch to the East Indies and to the Americas. [2] Similarly, coffee was banned by the Ethiopian Orthodox Church some time before the 18th century. [19]

question: when was coffee first made into a drink
gold_text: in the middle of the 15th century, in Yemen 's Sufi monasteries. [1] Coffee beans were first exported from Ethiopia to Yemen . Yemeni traders brought coffee back to their homeland and began to cultivate the bean. [13] The word qahwa originally meant wine, and Sufis in Yemen used the beverage as an aid to concentration and as a kind of spiritual intoxication when they chanted the name of God. [14] Sufis used it to keep themselves alert during their nighttime devotions. A translation of Al-Jaziri's manuscript [15] traces the spread of coffee from Arabia Felix (the present day Yemen) northward to Mecca and Medina , and then to the larger cities of Cairo , Damascus , Baghdad , and Constantinople . By 1414, the beverage was known in Mecca, and in the early 1500s was spreading to the Mameluke Sultanate of Egypt and North Africa from the Yemeni port of Mocha . [8] [14] Associated with Sufism , a myriad of coffee houses grew up in Cairo (Egypt) around the religious University of the Azhar. These coffee houses also opened in Syria, especially in the cosmopolitan city of Aleppo, [14] and then in Istanbul, the capital of the Ottoman Empire , in 1554. [14] In 1511, it was forbidden for its stimulating effect by conservative, orthodox imams at a theological court in Mecca . [16] However, these bans were to be overturned in 1524 by an order of the Ottoman Turkish Sultan Suleiman I , with Grand Mufti Mehmet Ebussuud el-İmadi issuing a fatwa allowing the consumption of coffee. [17] In Cairo , Egypt, a similar ban was instituted in 1532, and the coffeehouses and warehouses containing coffee beans were sacked. [18] During the 16th century, it had already reached the rest of the Middle East, the Safavid Empire and the Ottoman Empire . From the Middle East, coffee drinking spread to Italy, then to the rest of Europe, and coffee plants were transported by the Dutch to the East Indies and to the Americas. [2] Similarly, coffee was banned by the Ethiopian Orthodox Church some time before the 18th century. [19]

question: when was coffee first made into a drink
gold_text: in the middle of the 15th century, in Yemen 's Sufi monasteries. [1] Coffee beans were first exported from Ethiopia to Yemen . Yemeni traders brought coffee back to their homeland and began to cultivate the bean. [13] The word qahwa originally meant wine, and Sufis in Yemen used the beverage as an aid to concentration and as a kind of spiritual intoxication when they chanted the name of God. [14] Sufis used it to keep themselves alert during their nighttime devotions. A translation of Al-Jaziri's manuscript [15] traces the spread of coffee from Arabia Felix (the present day Yemen) northward to Mecca and Medina , and then to the larger cities of Cairo , Damascus , Baghdad , and Constantinople . By 1414, the beverage was known in Mecca, and in the early 1500s was spreading to the Mameluke Sultanate of Egypt and North Africa from the Yemeni port of Mocha . [8] [14] Associated with Sufism , a myriad of coffee houses grew up in Cairo (Egypt) around the religious University of the Azhar. These coffee houses also opened in Syria, especially in the cosmopolitan city of Aleppo, [14] and then in Istanbul, the capital of the Ottoman Empire , in 1554. [14] In 1511, it was forbidden for its stimulating effect by conservative, orthodox imams at a theological court in Mecca . [16] However, these bans were to be overturned in 1524 by an order of the Ottoman Turkish Sultan Suleiman I , with Grand Mufti Mehmet Ebussuud el-İmadi issuing a fatwa allowing the consumption of coffee. [17] In Cairo , Egypt, a similar ban was instituted in 1532, and the coffeehouses and warehouses containing coffee beans were sacked. [18] During the 16th century, it had already reached the rest of the Middle East, the Safavid Empire and the Ottoman Empire . From the Middle East, coffee drinking spread to Italy, then to the rest of Europe, and coffee plants were transported by the Dutch to the East Indies and to the Americas. [2] Similarly, coffee was banned by the Ethiopian Orthodox Church some time before the 18th century. [19]

The question of when coffee was first made into a drink can be traced back to the 15th century in Yemen, where coffee beans were first exported from Ethiopia. Yemeni traders brought the beans back to their homeland and began to cultivate them. The word "qahwa" originally meant wine, and Sufis in Yemen used the beverage as an aid to concentration and as a kind of spiritual intoxication when they chanted the name of God. The beverage was also used by Sufis to keep themselves alert during their nighttime devotions.

Coffee houses grew up in Cairo, Egypt, around the religious University of the Azhar, and then spread to other cities in the Middle East, the Safavid Empire, and the Ottoman Empire. In 1414, the beverage was known in Mecca, and in the early 1500s, it was spreading to the Mameluke Sultanate of Egypt and North Africa from the Yemeni port of Mocha. However, in 1511, it was forbidden for its stimulating effect by conservative, orthodox imams at a theological court in Mecca. This ban was overturned in 1524 by an order of the Ottoman Turkish Sultan Suleiman I, with Grand Mufti Mehmet Ebussuud el-İmadi issuing a fatwa allowing the consumption of coffee.

In Cairo, Egypt, a similar ban was instituted in 1532, and the coffeehouses and warehouses containing coffee beans were sacked. During the 16th century, coffee had already reached the rest of the Middle East, the Safavid Empire, and the Ottoman Empire. From the Middle East, coffee drinking spread to Italy, then to the rest of Europe, and coffee plants were transported by the Dutch to the East Indies and to the Americas.

Similarly, coffee was banned by the Ethiopian Orthodox Church some time before the 18th century.

question: when was coffee first made into a drink
gold_text: in the middle of the 15th century, in Yemen 's Sufi monasteries. [1] Coffee beans were first exported from Ethiopia to Yemen . Yemeni traders brought coffee back to their homeland and began to cultivate the bean. [13] The word qahwa originally meant wine, and Sufis in Yemen used the beverage as an aid to concentration and as a kind of spiritual intoxication when they chanted the name of God. [14] Sufis used it to keep themselves alert during their nighttime devotions. A translation of Al-Jaziri's manuscript [15] traces the spread of coffee from Arabia Felix (the present day Yemen) northward to Mecca and Medina , and then to the larger cities of Cairo , Damascus , Baghdad , and Constantinople . By 1414, the beverage was known in Mecca, and in the early 1500s was spreading to the Mameluke Sultanate of Egypt and North Africa from the Yemeni port of Mocha . [8] [14] Associated with Sufism , a myriad of coffee houses grew up in Cairo (Egypt) around the religious University of the Azhar. These coffee houses also opened in Syria, especially in the cosmopolitan city of Aleppo, [14] and then in Istanbul, the capital of the Ottoman Empire , in 1554. [14] In 1511, it was forbidden for its stimulating effect by conservative, orthodox imams at a theological court in Mecca . [16] However, these bans were to be overturned in 1524 by an order of the Ottoman Turkish Sultan Suleiman I , with Grand Mufti Mehmet Ebussuud el-İmadi issuing a fatwa allowing the consumption of coffee. [17] In Cairo , Egypt, a similar ban was instituted in 1532, and the coffeehouses and warehouses containing coffee beans were sacked. [18] During the 16th century, it had already reached the rest of the Middle East, the Safavid Empire and the Ottoman Empire . From the Middle East, coffee drinking spread to Italy, then to the rest of Europe, and coffee plants were transported by the Dutch to the East Indies and to the Americas. [2] Similarly, coffee was banned by the Ethiopian Orthodox Church some time before the 18th century. [19]

In Cairo, Egypt, a similar ban was instituted in 1532, and the coffeehouses and warehouses containing coffee beans were sacked. During the 16th century, it had already reached the rest of the Middle East, the Safavid Empire and the Ottoman Empire. From the Middle East, coffee drinking spread to Italy, then to the rest of Europe, and coffee plants were transported by the Dutch to the East Indies and to the Americas. question: when was coffee first made into a drink
gold_text: in the middle of the 15th century, in Yemen 's Sufi monasteries. [1] Coffee beans were first exported from Ethiopia to Yemen . Yemeni traders brought coffee back to their homeland and began to cultivate the bean. [13] The word qahwa originally meant wine, and Sufis in Yemen used the beverage as an aid to concentration and as a kind of spiritual intoxication when they chanted the name of God. [14] Sufis used it to keep themselves alert during their nighttime devotions. A translation of Al-Jaziri's manuscript [15] traces the spread of coffee from Arabia Felix (the present day Yemen) northward to Mecca and Medina , and then to the larger cities of Cairo , Damascus , Baghdad , and Constantinople . By 1414, the beverage was known in Mecca, and in the early 1500s was spreading to the Mameluke Sultanate of Egypt and North Africa from the Yemeni port of Mocha . [8] [14] Associated with Sufism , a myriad of coffee houses grew up in Cairo (Egypt) around the religious University of the Azhar. These coffee houses also opened in Syria, especially in the cosmopolitan city of Aleppo, [14] and then in Istanbul, the capital of the Ottoman Empire , in 1554. [14] In 1511, it was forbidden for its stimulating effect by conservative, orthodox imams at a theological court in Mecca . [16] However, these bans were to be overturned in 1524 by an order of the Ottoman Turkish Sultan Suleiman I , with Grand Mufti Mehmet Ebussuud el-İmadi issuing a fatwa allowing the consumption of coffee. [17] In Cairo , Egypt, a similar ban was instituted in 1532, and the coffeehouses and warehouses containing coffee beans were sacked. [18] During the 16th century, it had already reached the rest of the Middle East, the Safavid Empire and the Ottoman Empire . From the Middle East, coffee drinking spread to Italy, then to the rest of Europe, and coffee plants were transported by the Dutch to the East Indies and to the Americas. [2] Similarly, coffee was banned by the Ethiopian Orthodox Church some time before the 18th century. [19]

Yemeni traders brought the beans back to their homeland and began to cultivate them. By 1414, the beverage was known in Mecca, and in the early 1500s, it was spreading to the Mameluke Sultanate of Egypt and North Africa from the Yemeni port of Mocha. In 1511, it was forbidden for its stimulating effect by conservative, orthodox imams at a theological court in Mecca. However, these bans were overturned in 1524 by an order of the Ottoman Turkish Sultan Suleiman I, with Grand Mufti Mehmet Ebussuud el-İmadi issuing a fatwa allowing the consumption of coffee. During the 16th century, it had already reached the rest of the Middle East, the Safavid Empire, and the Ottoman Empire. question: when was coffee first made into a drink
gold_text: in the middle of the 15th century, in Yemen 's Sufi monasteries. [1] Coffee beans were first exported from Ethiopia to Yemen . Yemeni traders brought coffee back to their homeland and began to cultivate the bean. [13] The word qahwa originally meant wine, and Sufis in Yemen used the beverage as an aid to concentration and as a kind of spiritual intoxication when they chanted the name of God. [14] Sufis used it to keep themselves alert during their nighttime devotions. A translation of Al-Jaziri's manuscript [15] traces the spread of coffee from Arabia Felix (the present day Yemen) northward to Mecca and Medina , and then to the larger cities of Cairo , Damascus , Baghdad , and Constantinople . By 1414, the beverage was known in Mecca, and in the early 1500s was spreading to the Mameluke Sultanate of Egypt and North Africa from the Yemeni port of Mocha . [8] [14] Associated with Sufism , a myriad of coffee houses grew up in Cairo (Egypt) around the religious University of the Azhar. These coffee houses also opened in Syria, especially in the cosmopolitan city of Aleppo, [14] and then in Istanbul, the capital of the Ottoman Empire , in 1554. [14] In 1511, it was forbidden for its stimulating effect by conservative, orthodox imams at a theological court in Mecca . [16] However, these bans were to be overturned in 1524 by an order of the Ottoman Turkish Sultan Suleiman I , with Grand Mufti Mehmet Ebussuud el-İmadi issuing a fatwa allowing the consumption of coffee. [17] In Cairo , Egypt, a similar ban was instituted in 1532, and the coffeehouses and warehouses containing coffee beans were sacked. [18] During the 16th century, it had already reached the rest of the Middle East, the Safavid Empire and the Ottoman Empire . From the Middle East, coffee drinking spread to Italy, then to the rest of Europe, and coffee plants were transported by the Dutch to the East Indies and to the Americas. [2] Similarly, coffee was banned by the Ethiopian Orthodox Church some time before the 18th century. [19]

question: when was coffee first made into a drink
gold_text: in the middle of the 15th century, in Yemen 's Sufi monasteries. [1] Coffee beans were first exported from Ethiopia to Yemen . Yemeni traders brought coffee back to their homeland and began to cultivate the bean. [13] The word qahwa originally meant wine, and Sufis in Yemen used the beverage as an aid to concentration and as a kind of spiritual intoxication when they chanted the name of God. [14] Sufis used it to keep themselves alert during their nighttime devotions. A translation of Al-Jaziri's manuscript [15] traces the spread of coffee from Arabia Felix (the present day Yemen) northward to Mecca and Medina , and then to the larger cities of Cairo , Damascus , Baghdad , and Constantinople . By 1414, the beverage was known in Mecca, and in the early 1500s was spreading to the Mameluke Sultanate of Egypt and North Africa from the Yemeni port of Mocha . [8] [14] Associated with Sufism , a myriad of coffee houses grew up in Cairo (Egypt) around the religious University of the Azhar. These coffee houses also opened in Syria, especially in the cosmopolitan city of Aleppo, [14] and then in Istanbul, the capital of the Ottoman Empire , in 1554. [14] In 1511, it was forbidden for its stimulating effect by conservative, orthodox imams at a theological court in Mecca . [16] However, these bans were to be overturned in 1524 by an order of the Ottoman Turkish Sultan Suleiman I , with Grand Mufti Mehmet Ebussuud el-İmadi issuing a fatwa allowing the consumption of coffee. [17] In Cairo , Egypt, a similar ban was instituted in 1532, and the coffeehouses and warehouses containing coffee beans were sacked. [18] During the 16th century, it had already reached the rest of the Middle East, the Safavid Empire and the Ottoman Empire . From the Middle East, coffee drinking spread to Italy, then to the rest of Europe, and coffee plants were transported by the Dutch to the East Indies and to the Americas. [2] Similarly, coffee was banned by the Ethiopian Orthodox Church some time before the 18th century. [19]

The first mention of coffee as a drink is found in the middle of the 15th century in Yemen, where coffee beans were first exported from Ethiopia to Yemen. Yemeni traders brought the beans back to their homeland and began to cultivate them. The word "qahwa" originally meant wine, and Sufis in Yemen used the beverage as an aid to concentration and as a kind of spiritual intoxication when they chanted the name of God. Sufis used it to keep themselves alert during their nighttime devotions.

Coffee houses grew up in Cairo, Egypt, around the religious University of the Azhar, and then spread to Syria, especially in the cosmopolitan city of Aleppo. In 1414, the beverage was known in Mecca, and in the early 1500s, it was spreading to the Mameluke Sultanate of Egypt and North Africa from the Yemeni port of Mocha. In 1511, it was forbidden for its stimulating effect by conservative, orthodox imams at a theological court in Mecca. However, these bans were overturned in 1524 by an order of the Ottoman Turkish Sultan Suleiman I, with Grand Mufti Mehmet Ebussuud el-İmadi issuing a fatwa allowing the consumption of coffee.

Coffee houses and warehouses containing coffee beans were sacked in Cairo in 1532, and a similar ban was instituted in 1533 in Damascus. In 1554, coffee was brought to the Ottoman Empire, and by the end of the 16th century, it had reached the rest of the Middle East, the Safavid Empire, and the Ottoman Empire. From the Middle East, coffee drinking spread to Italy, then to the rest of Europe, and coffee plants were transported by the Dutch to the East Indies and to the Americas.

Coffee was banned by the Ethiopian Orthodox Church some time before the 18th century.

question: when was coffee first made into a drink
gold_text: in the middle of the 15th century, in Yemen 's Sufi monasteries. [1] Coffee beans were first exported from Ethiopia to Yemen . Yemeni traders brought coffee back to their homeland and began to cultivate the bean. [13] The word qahwa originally meant wine, and Sufis in Yemen used the beverage as an aid to concentration and as a kind of spiritual intoxication when they chanted the name of God. [14] Sufis used it to keep themselves alert during their nighttime devotions. A translation of Al-Jaziri's manuscript [15] traces the spread of coffee from Arabia Felix (the present day Yemen) northward to Mecca and Medina , and then to the larger cities of Cairo , Damascus , Baghdad , and Constantinople . By 1414, the beverage was known in Mecca, and in the early 1500s was spreading to the Mameluke Sultanate of Egypt and North Africa from the Yemeni port of Mocha . [8] [14] Associated with Sufism , a myriad of coffee houses grew up in Cairo (Egypt) around the religious University of the Azhar. These coffee houses also opened in Syria, especially in the cosmopolitan city of Aleppo, [14] and then in Istanbul, the capital of the Ottoman Empire , in 1554. [14] In 1511, it was forbidden for its stimulating effect by conservative, orthodox imams at a theological court in Mecca . [16] However, these bans were to be overturned in 1524 by an order of the Ottoman Turkish Sultan Suleiman I , with Grand Mufti Mehmet Ebussuud el-İmadi issuing a fatwa allowing the consumption of coffee. [17] In Cairo , Egypt, a similar ban was instituted in 1532, and the coffeehouses and warehouses containing coffee beans were sacked. [18] During the 16th century, it had already reached the rest of the Middle East, the Safavid Empire and the Ottoman Empire . From the Middle East, coffee drinking spread to Italy, then to the rest of Europe, and coffee plants were transported by the Dutch to the East Indies and to the Americas. [2] Similarly, coffee was banned by the Ethiopian Orthodox Church some time before the 18th century. [19]

question: when was coffee first made into a drink
gold_text: in the middle of the 15th century, in Yemen 's Sufi monasteries. [1] Coffee beans were first exported from Ethiopia to Yemen . Yemeni traders brought coffee back to their homeland and began to cultivate the bean. [13] The word qahwa originally meant wine, and Sufis in Yemen used the beverage as an aid to concentration and as a kind of spiritual intoxication when they chanted the name of God. [14] Sufis used it to keep themselves alert during their nighttime devotions. A translation of Al-Jaziri's manuscript [15] traces the spread of coffee from Arabia Felix (the present day Yemen) northward to Mecca and Medina , and then to the larger cities of Cairo , Damascus , Baghdad , and Constantinople . By 1414, the beverage was known in Mecca, and in the early 1500s was spreading to the Mameluke Sultanate of Egypt and North Africa from the Yemeni port of Mocha . [8] [14] Associated with Sufism , a myriad of coffee houses grew up in Cairo (Egypt) around the religious University of the Azhar. These coffee houses also opened in Syria, especially in the cosmopolitan city of Aleppo, [14] and then in Istanbul, the capital of the Ottoman Empire , in 1554. [14] In 1511, it was forbidden for its stimulating effect by conservative, orthodox imams at a theological court in Mecca . [16] However, these bans were to be overturned in 1524 by an order of the Ottoman Turkish Sultan Suleiman I , with Grand Mufti Mehmet Ebussuud el-İmadi issuing a fatwa allowing the consumption of coffee. [17] In Cairo , Egypt, a similar ban was instituted in 1532, and the coffeehouses and warehouses containing coffee beans were sacked. [18] During the 16th century, it had already reached the rest of the Middle East, the Safavid Empire and the Ottoman Empire . From the Middle East, coffee drinking spread to Italy, then to the rest of Europe, and coffee plants were transported by the Dutch to the East Indies and to the Americas. [2] Similarly, coffee was banned by the Ethiopian Orthodox Church some time before the 18th century. [19]

question: when was coffee first made into a drink
gold_text: in the middle of the 15th century, in Yemen 's Sufi monasteries. [1] Coffee beans were first exported from Ethiopia to Yemen . Yemeni traders brought coffee back to their homeland and began to cultivate the bean. [13] The word qahwa originally meant wine, and Sufis in Yemen used the beverage as an aid to concentration and as a kind of spiritual intoxication when they chanted the name of God. [14] Sufis used it to keep themselves alert during their nighttime devotions. A translation of Al-Jaziri's manuscript [15] traces the spread of coffee from Arabia Felix (the present day Yemen) northward to Mecca and Medina , and then to the larger cities of Cairo , Damascus , Baghdad , and Constantinople . By 1414, the beverage was known in Mecca, and in the early 1500s was spreading to the Mameluke Sultanate of Egypt and North Africa from the Yemeni port of Mocha . [8] [14] Associated with Sufism , a myriad of coffee houses grew up in Cairo (Egypt) around the religious University of the Azhar. These coffee houses also opened in Syria, especially in the cosmopolitan city of Aleppo, [14] and then in Istanbul, the capital of the Ottoman Empire , in 1554. [14] In 1511, it was forbidden for its stimulating effect by conservative, orthodox imams at a theological court in Mecca . [16] However, these bans were to be overturned in 1524 by an order of the Ottoman Turkish Sultan Suleiman I , with Grand Mufti Mehmet Ebussuud el-İmadi issuing a fatwa allowing the consumption of coffee. [17] In Cairo , Egypt, a similar ban was instituted in 1532, and the coffeehouses and warehouses containing coffee beans were sacked. [18] During the 16th century, it had already reached the rest of the Middle East, the Safavid Empire and the Ottoman Empire . From the Middle East, coffee drinking spread to Italy, then to the rest of Europe, and coffee plants were transported by the Dutch to the East Indies and to the Americas. [2] Similarly, coffee was banned by the Ethiopian Orthodox Church some time before the 18th century. [19]

The first mention of coffee as a drink can be traced back to the middle of the 15th century in Yemen, where coffee beans were first exported from Ethiopia to Yemen. Yemeni traders brought the coffee back to their homeland and began to cultivate the bean. The word "qahwa" originally meant wine, and Sufis in Yemen used the beverage as an aid to concentration and as a kind of spiritual intoxication when they chanted the name of God. Sufis used it to keep themselves alert during their nighttime devotions.

Coffee houses grew up in Cairo, Egypt, around the religious University of the Azhar, and then spread to Syria, especially in the cosmopolitan city of Aleppo. In 1414, the beverage was known in Mecca, and in the early 1500s, it was spreading to the Mameluke Sultanate of Egypt and North Africa from the Yemeni port of Mocha. By 1511, it was forbidden for its stimulating effect by conservative, orthodox imams at a theological court in Mecca. However, these bans were overturned in 1524 by an order of the Ottoman Turkish Sultan Suleiman I, with Grand Mufti Mehmet Ebussuud el-İmadi issuing a fatwa allowing the consumption of coffee.

In Cairo, Egypt, a similar ban was instituted in 1532, and the coffeehouses and warehouses containing coffee beans were sacked. During the 16th century, coffee had already reached the rest of the Middle East, the Safavid Empire, and the Ottoman Empire. From the Middle East, coffee drinking spread to Italy, then to the rest of Europe, and coffee plants were transported by the Dutch to the East Indies and to the Americas.

Similarly, coffee was banned by the Ethiopian Orthodox Church some time before the 18th century.

question: when was coffee first made into a drink
gold_text: in the middle of the 15th century, in Yemen 's Sufi monasteries. [1] Coffee beans were first exported from Ethiopia to Yemen . Yemeni traders brought coffee back to their homeland and began to cultivate the bean. [13] The word qahwa originally meant wine, and Sufis in Yemen used the beverage as an aid to concentration and as a kind of spiritual intoxication when they chanted the name of God. [14] Sufis used it to keep themselves alert during their nighttime devotions. A translation of Al-Jaziri's manuscript [15] traces the spread of coffee from Arabia Felix (the present day Yemen) northward to Mecca and Medina , and then to the larger cities of Cairo , Damascus , Baghdad , and Constantinople . By 1414, the beverage was known in Mecca, and in the early 1500s was spreading to the Mameluke Sultanate of Egypt and North Africa from the Yemeni port of Mocha . [8] [14] Associated with Sufism , a myriad of coffee houses grew up in Cairo (Egypt) around the religious University of the Azhar. These coffee houses also opened in Syria, especially in the cosmopolitan city of Aleppo, [14] and then in Istanbul, the capital of the Ottoman Empire , in 1554. [14] In 1511, it was forbidden for its stimulating effect by conservative, orthodox imams at a theological court in Mecca . [16] However, these bans were to be overturned in 1524 by an order of the Ottoman Turkish Sultan Suleiman I , with Grand Mufti Mehmet Ebussuud el-İmadi issuing a fatwa allowing the consumption of coffee. [17] In Cairo , Egypt, a similar ban was instituted in 1532, and the coffeehouses and warehouses containing coffee beans were sacked. [18] During the 16th century, it had already reached the rest of the Middle East, the Safavid Empire and the Ottoman Empire . From the Middle East, coffee drinking spread to Italy, then to the rest of Europe, and coffee plants were transported by the Dutch to the East Indies and to the Americas. [2] Similarly, coffee was banned by the Ethiopian Orthodox Church some time before the 18th century. [19]

question: when was coffee first made into a drink
gold_text: in the middle of the 15th century, in Yemen 's Sufi monasteries. [1] Coffee beans were first exported from Ethiopia to Yemen . Yemeni traders brought coffee back to their homeland and began to cultivate the bean. [13] The word qahwa originally meant wine, and Sufis in Yemen used the beverage as an aid to concentration and as a kind of spiritual intoxication when they chanted the name of God. [14] Sufis used it to keep themselves alert during their nighttime devotions. A translation of Al-Jaziri's manuscript [15] traces the spread of coffee from Arabia Felix (the present day Yemen) northward to Mecca and Medina , and then to the larger cities of Cairo , Damascus , Baghdad , and Constantinople . By 1414, the beverage was known in Mecca, and in the early 1500s was spreading to the Mameluke Sultanate of Egypt and North Africa from the Yemeni port of Mocha . [8] [14] Associated with Sufism , a myriad of coffee houses grew up in Cairo (Egypt) around the religious University of the Azhar. These coffee houses also opened in Syria, especially in the cosmopolitan city of Aleppo, [14] and then in Istanbul, the capital of the Ottoman Empire , in 1554. [14] In 1511, it was forbidden for its stimulating effect by conservative, orthodox imams at a theological court in Mecca . [16] However, these bans were to be overturned in 1524 by an order of the Ottoman Turkish Sultan Suleiman I , with Grand Mufti Mehmet Ebussuud el-İmadi issuing a fatwa allowing the consumption of coffee. [17] In Cairo , Egypt, a similar ban was instituted in 1532, and the coffeehouses and warehouses containing coffee beans were sacked. [18] During the 16th century, it had already reached the rest of the Middle East, the Safavid Empire and the Ottoman Empire . From the Middle East, coffee drinking spread to Italy, then to the rest of Europe, and coffee plants were transported by the Dutch to the East Indies and to the Americas. [2] Similarly, coffee was banned by the Ethiopian Orthodox Church some time before the 18th century. [19]

model_answer: The first person who charted the course of forgetting over time was Hermann Ebbinghaus, a German psychologist. In 1885, he published a paper titled "Über das Gedächtnis" (Memory: A Contribution to Experimental Psychology), in which he described his experiments on himself and the forgetting curve. Ebbinghaus discovered that people tend to halve their memory of newly learned knowledge in a matter of days or weeks unless they consciously review the learned material. This led to the development of the forgetting curve, which is now used to describe the rate at which information is lost over time when there is no attempt to retain it.

A typical graph of the forgetting curve purports to show that humans tend to halve their memory of newly learned knowledge in a matter of days or weeks unless they consciously review the learned material. The forgetting curve supports one of the seven kinds of memory failures: transience, which is the process of forgetting that occurs with the passage of time. Hermann Ebbinghaus ran a limited, incomplete study on himself and published his hypothesis in 1885 as Über das Gedächtnis (later translated into English as Memory: A Contribution to Experimental Psychology ). model_answer: The first person to chart the course of forgetting over time was Hermann Ebbinghaus, a German psychologist. In 1885, he published a paper titled "Über das Gedächtnis" (Memory: A Contribution to Experimental Psychology), in which he described his experiments on himself and the forgetting curve. Ebbinghaus discovered that people tend to halve their memory of newly learned knowledge in a matter of days or weeks unless they consciously review the learned material. This led to the development of the forgetting curve, which shows how information is lost over time when there is no attempt to retain it.

Ebbinghaus found that people tend to halve their memory of newly learned knowledge in a matter of days or weeks unless they consciously review the learned material. The forgetting curve supports the concept of transience, which is the process of forgetting that occurs with the passage of time.

Today, we approximate forgetting with an exponential curve [3] : R = e − t S , {\displaystyle R=e^{-{\frac {t}{S}}},} where R {\displaystyle R} is retrievability (a measure of how easy it is to retrieve a piece of information from memory), S {\displaystyle S} is stability of memory (determines how fast R {\displaystyle R} falls over time in the absence of training, testing or other recall), and t {\displaystyle t} is time. Hermann Ebbinghaus ran a limited, incomplete study on himself and published his hypothesis in 1885 as Über das Gedächtnis (later translated into English as Memory: A Contribution to Experimental Psychology ). Ebbinghaus studied the memorisation of nonsense syllables, such as "WID" and "ZOF" (CVCs or Consonant-Vowel-Consonant) by repeatedly testing himself after various time periods and recording the results. He plotted these results on a graph creating what is now known as the "forgetting curve". From his discovery regarding the "forgetting curve", Ebbinghaus came up with the effects of "overlearning". Essentially, if you practiced something more than what is usually necessary to memorize it, you would have effectively achieved overlearning. A typical graph of the forgetting curve purports to show that humans tend to halve their memory of newly learned knowledge in a matter of days or weeks unless they consciously review the learned material. The forgetting curve supports one of the seven kinds of memory failures: transience, which is the process of forgetting that occurs with the passage of time. Hermann Ebbinghaus ran a limited, incomplete study on himself and published his hypothesis in 1885 as Über das Gedächtnis (later translated into English as Memory: A Contribution to Experimental Psychology ). Ebbinghaus studied the memorisation of nonsense syllables, such as "WID" and "ZOF" (CVCs or Consonant-Vowel-Consonant) by repeatedly testing himself after various time periods and recording the results. Essentially, if you practiced something more than what is usually necessary to memorize it, you would have effectively achieved overlearning. In 1885, he published a paper titled "Über das Gedächtnis" (Memory: A Contribution to Experimental Psychology), in which he described his experiments on himself and the forgetting curve. Ebbinghaus found that people tend to halve their memory of newly learned knowledge in a matter of days or weeks unless they consciously review the learned material. This led to the development of the forgetting curve, which shows how information is lost over time when there is no attempt to retain it.

In 1885, he published a paper titled "Über das Gedächtnis" (Memory: A Contribution to Experimental Psychology), in which he described his experiments on himself and the forgetting curve. The forgetting curve shows how information is lost over time when there is no attempt to retain it. Ebbinghaus discovered that humans tend to halve their memory of newly learned knowledge in a matter of days or weeks unless they consciously review the learned material. This phenomenon is known as transience, one of the seven kinds of memory failures.

The forgetting curve supports one of the seven kinds of memory failures: transience, which is the process of forgetting that occurs with the passage of time. Hermann Ebbinghaus ran a limited, incomplete study on himself and published his hypothesis in 1885 as Über das Gedächtnis (later translated into English as Memory: A Contribution to Experimental Psychology ). Ebbinghaus studied the memorisation of nonsense syllables, such as "WID" and "ZOF" (CVCs or Consonant-Vowel-Consonant) by repeatedly testing himself after various time periods and recording the results. Essentially, if you practiced something more than what is usually necessary to memorize it, you would have effectively achieved overlearning. model_answer: The first person to chart the course of forgetting over time was Hermann Ebbinghaus, a German psychologist. In 1885, he published a paper titled "Über das Gedächtnis" (Memory: A Contribution to Experimental Psychology), in which he described his experiments on himself and the forgetting curve. Ebbinghaus found that people tend to halve their memory of newly learned knowledge in a matter of days or weeks unless they consciously review the learned material. This led to the development of the forgetting curve, which shows how information is lost over time when there is no attempt to retain it. The forgetting curve supports the concept of transience, which is the process of forgetting that occurs with the passage of time.

In 1885, he published a paper titled "Über das Gedächtnis" (Memory: A Contribution to Experimental Psychology), in which he described his experiments on himself and the forgetting curve. [1] A related concept is the strength of memory that refers to the durability that memory traces in the brain . The stronger the memory, the longer period of time that a person is able to recall it. A typical graph of the forgetting curve purports to show that humans tend to halve their memory of newly learned knowledge in a matter of days or weeks unless they consciously review the learned material. The forgetting curve supports one of the seven kinds of memory failures: transience, which is the process of forgetting that occurs with the passage of time. Hermann Ebbinghaus ran a limited, incomplete study on himself and published his hypothesis in 1885 as Über das Gedächtnis (later translated into English as Memory: A Contribution to Experimental Psychology ). Ebbinghaus studied the memorisation of nonsense syllables, such as "WID" and "ZOF" (CVCs or Consonant-Vowel-Consonant) by repeatedly testing himself after various time periods and recording the results. He plotted these results on a graph creating what is now known as the "forgetting curve". From his discovery regarding the "forgetting curve", Ebbinghaus came up with the effects of "overlearning". Essentially, if you practiced something more than what is usually necessary to memorize it, you would have effectively achieved overlearning. In 1885, he published a paper titled "Über das Gedächtnis" (Memory: A Contribution to Experimental Psychology), in which he described his experiments on himself and the forgetting curve. Ebbinghaus discovered that people tend to halve their memory of newly learned knowledge in a matter of days or weeks unless they consciously review the learned material. Hermann Ebbinghaus ran a limited, incomplete study on himself and published his hypothesis in 1885 as Über das Gedächtnis (later translated into English as Memory: A Contribution to Experimental Psychology ). Ebbinghaus studied the memorisation of nonsense syllables, such as "WID" and "ZOF" (CVCs or Consonant-Vowel-Consonant) by repeatedly testing himself after various time periods and recording the results. Essentially, if you practiced something more than what is usually necessary to memorize it, you would have effectively achieved overlearning. In 1885, he published a paper titled "Über das Gedächtnis" (Memory: A Contribution to Experimental Psychology), in which he described his experiments on himself and the forgetting curve he discovered. Ebbinghaus found that people tend to halve their memory of newly learned knowledge in a matter of days or weeks unless they consciously review the learned material. This forgetting curve supports the concept of transience, which is the process of forgetting that occurs with the passage of time.

The forgetting curve supports one of the seven kinds of memory failures: transience, which is the process of forgetting that occurs with the passage of time. Hermann Ebbinghaus ran a limited, incomplete study on himself and published his hypothesis in 1885 as Über das Gedächtnis (later translated into English as Memory: A Contribution to Experimental Psychology ). Ebbinghaus studied the memorisation of nonsense syllables, such as "WID" and "ZOF" (CVCs or Consonant-Vowel-Consonant) by repeatedly testing himself after various time periods and recording the results. He plotted these results on a graph creating what is now known as the "forgetting curve". From his discovery regarding the "forgetting curve", Ebbinghaus came up with the effects of "overlearning". Essentially, if you practiced something more than what is usually necessary to memorize it, you would have effectively achieved overlearning. In 1885, he published a paper titled "Über das Gedächtnis" (Memory: A Contribution to Experimental Psychology), in which he described his experiments on himself and the forgetting curve. Ebbinghaus discovered that people tend to halve their memory of newly learned knowledge in a matter of days or weeks unless they consciously review the learned material. This phenomenon is known as the forgetting curve, which supports the concept of transience, one of the seven kinds of memory failures. Ebbinghaus also introduced the idea of overlearning, which ensures that information is more impervious to being lost or forgotten by practicing it more than necessary.

Hermann Ebbinghaus ran a limited, incomplete study on himself and published his hypothesis in 1885 as Über das Gedächtnis (later translated into English as Memory: A Contribution to Experimental Psychology ). Ebbinghaus discovered that people tend to halve their memory of newly learned knowledge in a matter of days or weeks unless they consciously review the learned material. This phenomenon is known as the forgetting curve, which supports the concept of transience, one of the seven kinds of memory failures. model_answer: The first person to chart the course of forgetting over time was Hermann Ebbinghaus, who in 1885 published his findings on the forgetting curve. The forgetting curve shows how information is lost over time when there is no attempt to retain it. Ebbinghaus collected data on the memorization of nonsense syllables and plotted the results on a graph, creating what is now known as the "forgetting curve." He found that humans tend to halve their memory of newly learned knowledge in a matter of days or weeks unless they consciously review the learned material. The forgetting curve supports one of the seven kinds of memory failures: transience, which is the process of forgetting that occurs with the passage of time.

[1] A related concept is the strength of memory that refers to the durability that memory traces in the brain . The stronger the memory, the longer period of time that a person is able to recall it. A typical graph of the forgetting curve purports to show that humans tend to halve their memory of newly learned knowledge in a matter of days or weeks unless they consciously review the learned material. The forgetting curve supports one of the seven kinds of memory failures: transience, which is the process of forgetting that occurs with the passage of time. Hermann Ebbinghaus ran a limited, incomplete study on himself and published his hypothesis in 1885 as Über das Gedächtnis (later translated into English as Memory: A Contribution to Experimental Psychology ). Ebbinghaus studied the memorisation of nonsense syllables, such as "WID" and "ZOF" (CVCs or Consonant-Vowel-Consonant) by repeatedly testing himself after various time periods and recording the results. He plotted these results on a graph creating what is now known as the "forgetting curve". From his discovery regarding the "forgetting curve", Ebbinghaus came up with the effects of "overlearning". Essentially, if you practiced something more than what is usually necessary to memorize it, you would have effectively achieved overlearning. In 1885, he published a paper titled "Über das Gedächtnis" (Memory: A Contribution to Experimental Psychology), in which he described his experiments on himself and the forgetting curve. The forgetting curve shows how information is lost over time when there is no attempt to retain it. Ebbinghaus discovered that humans tend to halve their memory of newly learned knowledge in a matter of days or weeks unless they consciously review the learned material. This supports the concept of transience, which is the process of forgetting that occurs with the passage of time.

[1] A related concept is the strength of memory that refers to the durability that memory traces in the brain . The stronger the memory, the longer period of time that a person is able to recall it. A typical graph of the forgetting curve purports to show that humans tend to halve their memory of newly learned knowledge in a matter of days or weeks unless they consciously review the learned material. The forgetting curve supports one of the seven kinds of memory failures: transience, which is the process of forgetting that occurs with the passage of time. Hermann Ebbinghaus ran a limited, incomplete study on himself and published his hypothesis in 1885 as Über das Gedächtnis (later translated into English as Memory: A Contribution to Experimental Psychology ). Ebbinghaus studied the memorisation of nonsense syllables, such as "WID" and "ZOF" (CVCs or Consonant-Vowel-Consonant) by repeatedly testing himself after various time periods and recording the results. He plotted these results on a graph creating what is now known as the "forgetting curve". From his discovery regarding the "forgetting curve", Ebbinghaus came up with the effects of "overlearning". Essentially, if you practiced something more than what is usually necessary to memorize it, you would have effectively achieved overlearning. In 1885, he published a paper titled "Über das Gedächtnis" (Memory: A Contribution to Experimental Psychology), in which he described his experiments on himself and the forgetting curve. Ebbinghaus discovered that people tend to halve their memory of newly learned knowledge in a matter of days or weeks unless they consciously review the learned material. This phenomenon is known as the forgetting curve, which supports the concept of transience, one of the seven kinds of memory failures. Ebbinghaus also introduced the idea of overlearning, which involves practicing something more than what is usually necessary to memorize it, to ensure that information is more impervious to being lost or forgotten.

In 1885, he published a paper titled "Über das Gedächtnis" (Memory: A Contribution to Experimental Psychology), in which he described his experiments on himself and the forgetting curve. The forgetting curve shows how information is lost over time when there is no attempt to retain it. model_answer: One of the first to chart the course of forgetting over time was Hermann Ebbinghaus, a German psychologist. In 1885, he published his findings on the forgetting curve, which showed how information is lost over time when there is no attempt to retain it. Ebbinghaus collected data on the memorization of nonsense syllables and plotted the results on a graph, creating what is now known as the "forgetting curve." He found that humans tend to halve their memory of newly learned knowledge in a matter of days or weeks unless they consciously review the learned material. The forgetting curve supports one of the seven kinds of memory failures: transience, which is the process of forgetting that occurs with the passage of time. Ebbinghaus's research laid the groundwork for understanding the nature of forgetting and the importance of review and practice in retaining information.

After a series of supporting film and television roles in the late 1990s, she landed her breakthrough role as Bridget Hennessy on the ABC sitcom 8 Simple Rules , on which she starred from 2002 to 2005. Thereafter, Cuoco appeared as Billie Jenkins on the final season of the television series Charmed (2005–2006). Cuoco's film work includes roles in To Be Fat like Me (2007), Hop (2011) and Authors Anonymous (2014). She received a star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame in 2014. [2] In October 2017, Cuoco founded Yes, Norman Productions . One year olds are typically able to display the following skills:

* Physical and motor skills: Able to sit in a bucket, push a wheeled toy, and walk while holding onto furniture or walls.
* Sensory and cognitive development: Able to see near and far, interpret what is seen, and understand and learn language.
* Vocalization and socialization: Able to make sounds, babble, and communicate with others through sounds and gestures.

Two years olds are typically able to display the following skills:

* Motor development: Able to walk independently, run, and climb stairs.
* Sensory and cognitive development: Able to see, hear, and understand more complex language and concepts.
* Vocalization and socialization: Able to communicate more effectively, engage in parallel play, and interact with others.

Two and a half years olds are typically able to display the following skills:

* Motor development: Able to run, climb, and jump with ease.
* Sensory and cognitive development: Able to understand more complex language and concepts, and engage in pretend play.
* Vocalization and socialization: Able to communicate more effectively, engage in parallel play, and interact with others.

It is important to note that developmental milestones can vary greatly between individuals, and some children may reach these milestones at different ages.

The question of when a child is no longer a toddler is not a straightforward one, as there is no specific age or milestone that defines this transition. Toddler development is a gradual process, and children continue to grow and develop well into their teenage years. However, in general, toddlers are considered to be between the ages of 1 and 3, with 1-year-olds being the youngest group within this age range.

It is important to remember that every child develops at their own pace, and there is a wide range of normal developmental milestones for toddlers. Some common physical and motor skills for 1-year-olds include sitting up unassisted, crawling, and pulling themselves up to stand. Sensory and cognitive development also progresses rapidly during this time, with toddlers becoming more aware of their surroundings and beginning to understand simple concepts.

As children grow and develop, their abilities and interests continue to change and evolve. While there is no definitive age at which a child is no longer a toddler, it is generally accepted that the term refers to children between the ages of 1 and 3, with 1-year-olds being the youngest group within this age range.

The question of when a child is no longer a toddler is not a straightforward one, as there is no specific age or milestone that defines this transition. However, typically, children are considered toddlers until they reach the age of 3, and their developmental milestones are typically categorized as follows:

* 1 year old: Physical and motor skills, sensory and cognitive development, and vocalization and socialization.
* 2 years old: Motor development, play (parallel play), and major learning events such as toilet training and language development.
* 3 years old: Vocalization and socialization, and major learning events such as toilet training and language development.

It is important to note that developmental milestones can vary greatly between children, and some may reach certain milestones earlier or later than others. Additionally, children may continue to develop and grow beyond the age of 3, and their development may not necessarily follow a linear path.

question: what is the main mineral in lithium batteries
gold_text: exchangers that are prone to corrosion. The reactors use lithium to counteract the corrosive effects of boric acid , which is added to the water to absorb excess neutrons. [139] Medicine [ edit ] Main article: Lithium (medication) Lithium is useful in the treatment of bipolar disorder . [140] Lithium salts may also be helpful for related diagnoses, such as schizoaffective disorder and cyclic major depression . The active part of these salts is the lithium ion Li + . [140] They may increase the risk of developing Ebstein's cardiac anomaly in infants born to women who take lithium during the first trimester of pregnancy. [141] Lithium has also been researched as a possible treatment for cluster headaches . [142] Biological role [ edit ] Primary food sources of lithium are grains and vegetables, and, in some areas, drinking water also contains significant amounts. [143] Human intake varies depending on location and diet. Lithium was first detected in human organs and fetal tissues in the late 19th century. In humans there are no defined lithium deficiency diseases, but low lithium intakes from water supplies were associated with increased rates of suicides, homicides and the arrest rates for drug use and other crimes. The biochemical mechanisms of action of lithium appear to be multifactorial and are intercorrelated with the functions of several enzymes, hormones and vitamins, as well as with growth and transforming factors. Evidence now appears to be sufficient to accept lithium as essential; a provisional RDA of 1,000 µg/day is suggested for a 70 kg adult. [143] [144] Precautions [ edit ] NFPA 704 fire diamond 3 2 2 W Fire diamond hazard sign for lithium metal [145] Lithium is corrosive and requires special handling to avoid skin contact. Breathing lithium dust or lithium compounds (which are often alkaline) initially irritate the nose and throat, while higher exposure can cause a buildup of fluid in the lungs , leading to pulmonary edema . The metal itself is a handling hazard because contact with moisture produces the caustic lithium hydroxide. Lithium is safely stored in non-reactive compounds such as naphtha . [146] Regulation [ edit ] Some jurisdictions limit the sale of lithium batteries , which are the most readily available source of lithium for ordinary consumers. Lithium

[139] Medicine [ edit ] Main article: Lithium (medication) Lithium is useful in the treatment of bipolar disorder . [140] Lithium salts may also be helpful for related diagnoses, such as schizoaffective disorder and cyclic major depression . The active part of these salts is the lithium ion Li + . [140] They may increase the risk of developing Ebstein's cardiac anomaly in infants born to women who take lithium during the first trimester of pregnancy. [141] Lithium has also been researched as a possible treatment for cluster headaches . [142] Biological role [ edit ] Primary food sources of lithium are grains and vegetables, and, in some areas, drinking water also contains significant amounts. [143] Human intake varies depending on location and diet. Lithium was first detected in human organs and fetal tissues in the late 19th century. In humans there are no defined lithium deficiency diseases, but low lithium intakes from water supplies were associated with increased rates of suicides, homicides and the arrest rates for drug use and other crimes. The biochemical mechanisms of action of lithium appear to be multifactorial and are intercorrelated with the functions of several enzymes, hormones and vitamins, as well as with growth and transforming factors. Evidence now appears to be sufficient to accept lithium as essential; a provisional RDA of 1,000 µg/day is suggested for a 70 kg adult. [143] [144] Precautions [ edit ] NFPA 704 fire diamond 3 2 2 W Fire diamond hazard sign for lithium metal [145] Lithium is corrosive and requires special handling to avoid skin contact. Breathing lithium dust or lithium compounds (which are often alkaline) initially irritate the nose and throat, while higher exposure can cause a buildup of fluid in the lungs , leading to pulmonary edema . The metal itself is a handling hazard because contact with moisture produces the caustic lithium hydroxide. Lithium is safely stored in non-reactive compounds such as naphtha .
